title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: Coronary atherosclerosis is increasingly recognized as a chronic, maladaptive inflammatory disease initiated by arterial retention of apolipoprotein B (apoB)–containing lipoproteins and amplified by innate and adaptive immune responses. Although low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) remains a central causal factor, substantial residual risk persists despite intensive LDL-C lowering, emphasizing the clinical relevance of residual inflammatory risk and additional atherogenic lipid metrics such as apolipoprotein B (apoB), remnant cholesterol, small dense LDL, and lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]. Landmark outcome trials validate both paradigms: potent lipid-lowering therapies reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, and targeted anti-inflammatory therapies such as IL-1β inhibition and low-dose colchicine reduce recurrent events without altering LDL-C, establishing inflammation as a modifiable driver of coronary risk. This review integrates mechanistic evidence linking lipids and

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: altering LDL-C, establishing inflammation as a modifiable driver of coronary risk. This review integrates mechanistic evidence linking lipids and inflammation across the atherosclerotic continuum—from endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment to plaque destabilization and thrombosis—while critically appraising biomarkers, imaging approaches, and therapeutic strategies. We propose a practical dual-axis framework integrating residual cholesterol and inflammatory risks to guide combined therapy and highlight future directions including genetics-informed lipid management [notably Lp(a)], inflammation-resolution biology, and precision targeting of upstream inflammatory pathways such as IL-6 signaling.

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: 8 Discussion This review supports a clinically useful synthesis: coronary risk is best understood through interacting but non-identical axes of apoB particle burden, inflammatory pathway activation, and failure of resolution. The key translational task is therefore not to restate these mechanisms, but to match them to patient selection, biomarker choice, and implementable treatment sequencing. Integration of genetics [Lp(a), polygenic risk], immune programming (trained immunity/CHIP), and imaging-defined plaque phenotype may further refine precision targeting, but only if workflows are cost-effective and improve outcomes beyond guideline-based care ( 16 , 17 , 50 – 53 , 56 – 60 , 63 – 65 , 67 , 68 , 85 – 89 ). Pragmatic trials embedded in healthcare systems and implementation science will therefore be essential to translate dual-axis strategies into durable reductions in coronary events. The next phase of coronary prevention research should prioritize bridging mechanistic insights to

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: into durable reductions in coronary events. The next phase of coronary prevention research should prioritize bridging mechanistic insights to scalable implementation ( 4 – 6 , 15 – 23 , 25 – 27 , 35 , 38 , 39 , 43 , 67 , 68 ). First, trials should prespecify stratification around apoB/non–HDL-C, hsCRP/IL-6 pathway activity, Lp(a), and imaging-defined plaque phenotype so that the biology driving benefit can be identified rather than inferred post hoc . Second, biomarker selection should be pathway-matched: hsCRP for broad inflammatory enrichment, IL-6-axis markers when cytokine targeting is contemplated, apoB or remnant-related markers when particle exposure is central, and lesion imaging when local plaque phenotype is likely to alter treatment sequencing. Third, resolution biology requires standardized measurement—SPM panels, efferocytosis signatures, and lesion-level readouts—to move from concept to intervention. 8.1 Why triglyceride lowering does not always translate into event

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: signatures, and lesion-level readouts—to move from concept to intervention. 8.1 Why triglyceride lowering does not always translate into event reduction Future TRL trials should quantify apoB and remnant-C change ( 90 – 95 ), stratify by metabolic phenotype, and include intermediate endpoints consistent with reduced inflammatory stimulation. Clinically, this argues for evidence-based selection of therapies rather than assuming that all triglyceride-lowering strategies are equivalent. Genetic and mechanistic evidence supports remnant/TRL causality, yet trials differ because interventions vary in whether they reduce apoB-containing particle exposure and whether they modulate inflammatory coupling. Triglyceride concentration is a surrogate; reductions do not necessarily imply fewer atherogenic particles or less arterial retention. 8.2 Immunothrombosis as the final common pathway to acute coronary syndromes Translational priorities include standardization of immunothrombotic biomarkers

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: as the final common pathway to acute coronary syndromes Translational priorities include standardization of immunothrombotic biomarkers and ( 96 – 101 ) validation of targets that reduce thrombosis without compromising host defense. In the near term, indirect modulation—via substrate removal and pathway-relevant inflammatory control—remains the most feasible route to reduce immunothrombotic propensity. The conversion of plaque inflammation into thrombosis is the proximate cause of acute coronary syndromes. NETs, platelet activation, endothelial injury, and coagulation form a feed-forward network that couples inflammatory effector programs to thrombus formation. 8.3 Resolution biology—therapeutic promise and measurement challenges A major gap is measurement: scalable clinical surrogates of resolution are lacking ( 61 , 102 – 106 ). Developing validated resolution biomarkers and imaging endpoints will be essential for translating resolution-enhancing strategies and for determining

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: validated resolution biomarkers and imaging endpoints will be essential for translating resolution-enhancing strategies and for determining whether they can stabilize plaques with fewer safety trade-offs than cytokine inhibition. Resolution is an active program that terminates inflammation and promotes repair, mediated by specialized pro-resolving mediators and efficient efferocytosis. Resolution failure provides a mechanistically coherent explanation for necrotic core expansion and plaque vulnerability. 8.4 Genetics-informed prevention and the special case of lipoprotein(a) Therapeutic pipelines—ASO/siRNA approaches and oral particle-formation inhibition—are ( 107 – 112 ) progressing quickly. Outcomes trials will define the required magnitude and duration of lowering and identify the highest-yield clinical populations for implementation. Lp(a) identifies inherited residual risk and integrates atherogenic, inflammatory, and potentially prothrombotic biology. At least one lifetime

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: Lp(a) identifies inherited residual risk and integrates atherogenic, inflammatory, and potentially prothrombotic biology. At least one lifetime Lp(a) measurement is practical and can trigger earlier and more intensive management of modifiable risks, including aggressive apoB exposure reduction. 8.5 Upstream hematopoiesis—trained immunity and clonal hematopoiesis (CHIP) Translation will require scalable phenotyping and clear thresholds for intervention ( 113 – 117 ). If upstream inflammatory inhibition proves effective and safe, immune-programming–enriched phenotypes may become high-yield targets for precision prevention strategies. Trained immunity and CHIP highlight that residual inflammatory risk can reflect durable immune programming, not just transient biomarker elevation. These mechanisms may help explain persistent inflammation in older patients and variability in response to standard lipid lowering. 8.6 Imaging endpoints as translational bridges The key implementation question

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: older patients and variability in response to standard lipid lowering. 8.6 Imaging endpoints as translational bridges The key implementation question is when imaging changes management. A pragmatic model ( 66 , 118 – 121 ) is biomarker-first risk phenotyping with selective imaging for discordant cases, recurrent events, or research settings evaluating new therapies. Imaging quantifies plaque burden and vulnerability features, providing a bridge between mechanisms and clinical phenotypes. CTA enables noninvasive phenotyping; IVUS/OCT provide high-resolution characterization in selected patients undergoing invasive evaluation. 8.7 Implementation priorities for the next generation of trials and guidelines Trial design should increasingly incorporate enrichment for residual-risk phenotypes ( 122 – 127 ), verification of on-target pathway modulation, and intermediate endpoints that map to mechanisms (plaque composition, inflammatory signatures, or resolution readouts). These steps will

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: modulation, and intermediate endpoints that map to mechanisms (plaque composition, inflammatory signatures, or resolution readouts). These steps will help translate mechanistic advances into durable reductions in coronary events on top of contemporary background care. Across lipid and inflammation domains, the highest-yield near-term priority is phenotype-guided treatment pathways that are measurable, safe, and scalable. This includes harmonized use of apoB/non–HDL-C for particle burden, routine Lp(a) testing at least once, repeated hsCRP assessment when inflammatory targeting is considered, and selective imaging when it can change treatment intensity or sequencing. 8.8 Outstanding controversies and near-term priorities This field is advancing rapidly ( 33 – 131 ), but several issues remain unsettled. First, the magnitude of benefit achievable by adding anti-inflammatory therapy on top of modern intensive lipid lowering—and the patient groups in whom benefit clearly outweighs

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: achievable by adding anti-inflammatory therapy on top of modern intensive lipid lowering—and the patient groups in whom benefit clearly outweighs risk—requires clearer definition. Second, triglyceride-lowering strategies continue to yield heterogeneous trial results, emphasizing the need to focus on particle burden and causal pathways rather than triglycerides alone. Third, for Lp(a) therapies, the magnitude and duration of lowering required for event reduction remain to be proven. Finally, scalable phenotyping tools for plaque inflammation and resolution are still evolving, limiting precision targeting in routine care. 8.9 Research agenda: bridging mechanism to implementation To better bridge mechanism to implementation, future trials should routinely quantify both particle exposure and inflammatory activity, including apoB/non–HDL-C as substrate metrics and hsCRP with pathway-specific markers (e.g., IL-6 signaling) when relevant, so that biological on-target effects can be linked to

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: substrate metrics and hsCRP with pathway-specific markers (e.g., IL-6 signaling) when relevant, so that biological on-target effects can be linked to plaque phenotypes and clinical outcomes ( 16 , 20 , 21 , 38 , 39 , 77 , 132 – 135 ). In parallel, ( 18 , 19 , 35 – 50 , 65 , 67 , 68 ) the field needs scalable readouts of resolution biology and immunothrombosis, and pragmatic health-system workflows that support adherence, rapid intensification for very-high-risk phenotypes, and equitable access to advanced therapies ( 136 – 139 ). 8.10 Take-home messages for clinicians and investigators First, apoB-containing lipoproteins initiate coronary disease by arterial retention; therefore, exposure reduction remains the most reliable strategy for durable risk reduction ( 4 – 6 , 15 – 17 , 20 , 21 , 24 , 35 , 38 , 39 , 43 , 44 , 46 , 54 – 60 , 63 – 65 , 67 , 68 ). LDL-C is a useful target, but apoB and non–HDL-C can better reflect particle burden when discordance is likely, and remnant-C and

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: – 65 , 67 , 68 ). LDL-C is a useful target, but apoB and non–HDL-C can better reflect particle burden when discordance is likely, and remnant-C and Lp(a) refine residual cholesterol risk. Second, residual inflammatory risk is real and modifiable, but pathway specificity and safety determine clinical usefulness ( 11 – 14 , 35 , 38 – 43 , 73 ). hsCRP is a practical screening tool, while the IL-6 axis represents a leading upstream target under outcomes testing; however, anti-inflammatory therapy should be reserved for patients in whom the inflammatory signal is reproducible and the expected benefit outweighs infection, tolerability, and interaction-related risks. Third, the lipid and inflammation hypotheses should be operationalized as complementary axes rather than competing explanations ( 3 – 6 , 15 – 23 , 43 , 85 – 89 ). Patients high on both axes have the greatest absolute benefit potential from combined strategies, whereas discordant profiles call for more selective escalation.

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: on both axes have the greatest absolute benefit potential from combined strategies, whereas discordant profiles call for more selective escalation. Fourth, implementation matters: scalable workflows—apoB/non–HDL-C for particle burden, lifetime Lp(a) testing, repeated hsCRP in selected patients, and selective imaging when it changes management—are available today and can improve clinical decisions even before next-generation therapies mature ( 140 – 142 ). 8.11 Cost, equity, and health-system implementation: making precision prevention scalable Embedding these tiers into health-system workflows—standardized order sets, decision support based on structured residual-risk phenotyping, and follow-up reminders—can improve adherence and persistence, which are often the main determinants of long-term benefit ( 23 , 35 , 41 , 43 – 46 ). Such implementation science is essential to translate rapidly expanding lipid–inflammation biology into durable reductions in coronary events across diverse

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: science is essential to translate rapidly expanding lipid–inflammation biology into durable reductions in coronary events across diverse patient populations. A pragmatic approach is tiered implementation ( 4 – 6 , 15 – 17 , 20 , 21 , 56 – 60 , 63 – 65 , 67 , 68 ). Tier 1 uses universally available tools: statins, ezetimibe, blood pressure and glycemic control, smoking cessation, and measurement of LDL-C/non–HDL-C and hsCRP in selected patients. Tier 2 adds apoB and Lp(a) testing where available to refine exposure and inherited risk ( 142 ). Tier 3 adds higher-cost therapies and selective imaging for the highest-risk phenotypes [recurrent events, high plaque burden, high Lp(a), persistent inflammatory risk] where absolute benefit is greatest ( 136 , 140 , 141 ). Many of the most effective contemporary therapies—PCSK9 inhibition, long-acting RNA-based agents, and emerging Lp(a)-lowering modalities—raise cost and access challenges ( 8 , 9 , 56 – 60 , 63 – 65 , 78 , 79 ). If precision

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: RNA-based agents, and emerging Lp(a)-lowering modalities—raise cost and access challenges ( 8 , 9 , 56 – 60 , 63 – 65 , 78 , 79 ). If precision prevention is implemented only in highly resourced settings, population-level event reduction will be limited. Therefore, a translational review should explicitly acknowledge that scalability and equity are part of the scientific problem: mechanisms only matter clinically when they can be acted upon ( 136 , 140 , 143 ).

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: 9 Conclusion Coronary atherosclerosis should be managed as a disease of retained apoB-containing particles, maladaptive inflammation, and their interaction within the plaque microenvironment. In practice, the most defensible sequence is to lower apoB exposure first and durably, then determine whether clinically meaningful inflammatory activity persists, and finally use selective imaging when lesion-level information is likely to change treatment intensity or sequencing. ApoB/non–HDL-C, remnant-related measures, one-time Lp(a) testing, and hsCRP each add value when they are matched to the biological question they are meant to answer. Future progress will depend less on repeating the concept of residual risk and more on converting it into a workable clinical workflow. The next phase should prioritize explicit patient stratification, pathway-matched therapy, confirmation that the intended biology has actually been modified, and pragmatic delivery models that preserve safety, adherence,

title: Inflammation and lipid-related determinants in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic implications
text: therapy, confirmation that the intended biology has actually been modified, and pragmatic delivery models that preserve safety, adherence, and access. Ongoing IL-6-pathway, TRL-targeting, and Lp(a)-lowering trials may refine this framework, but current practice should remain anchored in durable apoB reduction, selective biomarker-guided anti-inflammatory escalation, and implementation strategies that make effective therapy sustainable in routine care.

title: Predictive value of ALBI score in assessing prognosis of NSTEMI: a retrospective cohort study
text: Objective This study aims to evaluate the predictive value of the albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score for mortality risk in patients with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 982 patients with NSTEMI. A multivariate Cox proportional hazards model was established to analyze the predictive value of ALBI for mortality after hospital discharge in NSTEMI patients. Additionally, restricted cubic spline (RCS) plots were used to analyze the relationship between ALBI and post-discharge mortality. Operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated to assess the predictive accuracy of ALBI, and nomograms were constructed to facilitate clinical application in predicting mortality after hospital discharge in patients with NSTEMI. Results Among the 982 participants, 62 (6.3%) developed death during the follow-up. In unadjusted Cox regression models, the ALBI index had a hazard ratio (HR) of 5.07 (95% confidence interval CI:

title: Predictive value of ALBI score in assessing prognosis of NSTEMI: a retrospective cohort study
text: death during the follow-up. In unadjusted Cox regression models, the ALBI index had a hazard ratio (HR) of 5.07 (95% confidence interval CI: 3.13–8.20, P < 0.001). In the adjusted models, the relationship still persisted. Furthmore, a non-linear and dose–response relationship between the ALBI index and the primary endpoint was observed (non-linear P = 0.050, P overall < 0.001). ROC curve analysis revealed good predictive performance for ALBI. The nomogram model correctly separates patients with and without death risk, with an AUC of 0.835. Our model showed improved prediction of death compared to GRACE, or NT-proBNP (all P < 0.05). Conclusion ALBI was significantly associated with the risk of out-of-hospital death in NSTEMI patients. The novel nomogram based on ALBI, NT-proBNP, and GRACE scores showed an improvement in predicting mortality.

The GRACE Score ( 11 , 16 ) was a risk stratification model for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) developed based on the Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events. text: Discussion The present study, data from a real-world registry, aimed to assess the potential of combining ALBI with GRACE for improving risk stratification for NSTEMI patients. The main conclusions were as follows: (1) Elevated ALBI levels were significantly associated with a greater risk of all-cause death in NSTEMI patients; (2) RCS analysis indicates that ALBI was positively correlated with all-cause mortality risk in NSTEMI patients. ROC analysis demonstrates its strong predictive capability for mortality risk in NSTEMI patients.; and (3) Adding ALBI and NT-proBNP to GRACE score models can significantly enhance the ability to predict all-cause death outcomes. Oxidative stress, inflammation, and nutritional status are important pathophysiological mechanisms of AMI, closely related to its occurrence and progression. Previous studies have confirmed that factors such as white blood cells, neutrophils ( 19 ), TNF-α, IL-6 ( 20 ), and C-reactive protein ( 21 ) are closely associated with

text: confirmed that factors such as white blood cells, neutrophils ( 19 ), TNF-α, IL-6 ( 20 ), and C-reactive protein ( 21 ) are closely associated with the severity of AMI and long-term prognosis, gradually becoming important markers for evaluating the progression of AMI. Serum albumin is a marker of inflammation and nutrition ( 22 ). As a major component of plasma, albumin has long been considered an important indicator of nutritional status. However, increasing evidence suggests that albumin levels can reflect the degree of systemic inflammation, organ (e.g., heart, kidney, liver) function, and the severity of many diseases ( 23 ). Studies have shown that low serum albumin levels are associated with poor prognosis in AMI and chronic coronary artery disease ( 24 ). In AMI patients, reduced serum albumin at admission is linked to in-hospital outcomes, long-term survival in myocardial infarction patients, and no-reflow after primary percutaneous intervention. ( 25 ) conducted a retrospective study, and the results showed that the cumulative incidence of the main composite events was higher in the group with hypoalbuminemia. After adjusting for relevant clinical variables, hypoalbuminemia remained an independent predictor. Some researchers also conducted cross-sectional studies, and the results showed that a lower serum albumin concentration was associated with the first occurrence of acute myocardial infarction ( 26 ). In a study following 2,305 first-onset AMI patients and found that low serum albumin levels at admission were independent predictors of long-term all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and cardiac mortality in these patients ( 27 ). Bilirubin, as an endogenous antioxidant, exhibits antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective effects ( 28 ). The bilirubin can suppress nonspecific inflammation, reducing the production of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-γ, and prevent the oxidation of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), thereby mitigating systemic inflammation and oxidative stress damage ( 29 ). Munire et al. ( 30 ) studied 615 STEMI patients undergoing PCI and found that the bilirubin level was higher in the MACE group (17.21 ± 6.49 mmol/L vs. 13.34 ± 4.91 mmol/L, P < 0.001), and the post-PCI TIMI flow grade was lower ( P = 0.023). There are scholars observed that the high-bilirubin group had significantly higher in-hospital mortality and MACE rates ( P < 0.001) ( 31 ). A comprehensive analysis identified that the

title: Predictive value of ALBI score in assessing prognosis of NSTEMI: a retrospective cohort study
text: high-bilirubin group had significantly higher in-hospital mortality and MACE rates ( P < 0.001) ( 31 ). A comprehensive analysis identified that the high-bilirubin group had a higher incidence of MACE (16.9% vs. 5.6%, P < 0.001) and cardiac mortality (15.3% vs. 4.5%, P < 0.001) compared to the low-bilirubin group ( 32 ). Elevated bilirubin levels may reflect chronic inflammation and increased oxidative stress. However, some scholars have reached different conclusions in their research. A follow-up study of 4,151 STEMI patients undergoing PPCI found that the high-TBil group had significantly lower MACE rates than the low-TBil group (3.5% vs. 11.0%, P = 0.001) ( 33 ). Wei et al. reported that MACE patients had lower bilirubin levels (18.3 ± 6.7 vs. 14.8 ± 6.6 mg/L, P < 0.01) ( 34 ). The findings are inconsistent, and our results also did not reveal significant abnormalities, suggesting that bilirubin alone may not be a robust predictor of AMI prognosis. The ALBI score provides a more stable and integrated indicator of overall pathological burden by combining bilirubin with albumin. This score captures elements of acute and chronic injury (via bilirubin) while reflecting concomitant functional reserve (via albumin), providing a more robust composite measure of inflammation, oxidative stress, and nutritional status than any single marker. It can be integrated into routine clinical assessments to rapidly evaluate mortality risk for patients with conditions such as acute myocardial infarction, complementing existing tools like the GRACE score. title: Pediatric Critical Illness, Immunometabolism and Cardiovascular Risk: A Narrative Review
text: The management of critical illness has significantly advanced, enabling a greater number of patients to survive conditions that were once fatal. However, survival often comes at a cost, as many patients experience long-term sequelae, including chronic critical illness (CCI) and post-intensive care syndrome (PICS). These syndromes can also be subclinical, driven by a persistent imbalance between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory processes, resulting in sustained immune dysfunction, metabolic disturbances, and organ-specific complications. Among the most affected systems are the immune and cardiovascular systems, which undergo acute metabolic shifts during critical illness to meet energy demands. However, if unresolved, these shifts can support chronic inflammation and dysfunction. Failed resolution of inflammation may contribute to long-term cardiovascular disease (CVD), including hypertension and atherosclerosis, through impaired vascular integrity and healing. Clinical and animal

title: Pediatric Critical Illness, Immunometabolism and Cardiovascular Risk: A Narrative Review
text: cardiovascular disease (CVD), including hypertension and atherosclerosis, through impaired vascular integrity and healing. Clinical and animal studies demonstrate that acute inflammatory insults, such as trauma or severe infections, can trigger sustained vascular inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and maladaptive immune responses, leading to an elevated risk of early-onset CVD. This review explores the interplay between immune dysregulation and cardiovascular outcomes in survivors of critical illness, particularly in children and young adults. It highlights the role of metabolic reprogramming, immune-mediated inflammation, and specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) in both the acute and chronic phases of recovery. Current evidence and studies that provide a link between acute critical illness and immune and cardiovascular sequelae are discussed.

title: Pediatric Critical Illness, Immunometabolism and Cardiovascular Risk: A Narrative Review
text: Conclusion Recent advancements in managing the acute phases of critical illness have resulted in a decreased mortality via improved support of organ failure, leading to a growing number of patients surviving previously fatal insults. However, a growing body of literature suggests that the survival of an acute challenge may not end its impact on health, even in previously healthy populations such as children and adolescents. This has become increasingly clear with the evolution and definition of new subpopulations of critical illness, such as CCI and PICS, where the pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory processes have not fully abated. Extensive additional work will be required to improve the recognition of this process, as well as our ability to identify individuals at particularly high risk. Treatment will depend on the development of specific mechanisms to “reset” this vascular inflammatory response and return the cardiovascular system to its pre-morbid state. This may include

text: of specific mechanisms to “reset” this vascular inflammatory response and return the cardiovascular system to its pre-morbid state. This may include aggressive lifestyle and dietary interventions and/or treatment with anti-inflammatory pharmaceuticals.

title: A review of the protection mechanisms of ginsenoside CK on cardiovascular disease and stroke
text: Cardiovascular disease (CVD), comprising coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, heart failure, and hypertension, predominantly originates from dysfunction or obstruction within the cardiac and vascular systems. It has persistently remained the leading cause of death worldwide. The classification of stroke is based on its pathogenesis, with ischemic and hemorrhagic types representing distinct classifications. The etiology of stroke is attributed to cerebral vascular occlusion or rupture. It is frequently associated with hypoxic injury and neuronal necrosis, which poses a significant burden on individuals and public health systems. Ginsenoside compound K (CK), a secondary metabolite derived from the intestinal microbial transformation of protopanaxadiol type ginsenosides (e.g., Rb1, Rb2), exhibits high oral bioavailability and the capacity to cross the blood-brain barrier. Recent research has demonstrated that CK possesses antiplatelet and antithrombotic activities,

title: A review of the protection mechanisms of ginsenoside CK on cardiovascular disease and stroke
text: and the capacity to cross the blood-brain barrier. Recent research has demonstrated that CK possesses antiplatelet and antithrombotic activities, inhibits vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and endothelial inflammation, and shows low toxicity along with antiarrhythmic potential in the cardiovascular system. Furthermore, CK demonstrates significant anti-inflammatory, antioxidative, and mitochondrial protective properties, exhibiting efficacy in models of myocardial ischemia/reperfusion and cerebral ischemia. It exhibits good tolerability and safety without significant antagonism to other drugs and is increasingly recognized as a promising multi-target natural therapeutic candidate. The objective of this review is twofold: first, to synthesize recent findings on the mechanisms by which ginsenoside CK confers protection in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular conditions; and second, to assess its translational potential and highlight its prospective role in next-generation

title: A review of the protection mechanisms of ginsenoside CK on cardiovascular disease and stroke
text: and cerebrovascular conditions; and second, to assess its translational potential and highlight its prospective role in next-generation cardiovascular therapies.

text: 5 Discussion The therapeutic potential of CK in cardiovascular and cerebrovascular protection is firmly supported by its diverse mechanistic pathways, ranging from antioxidant defense to anti-inflammatory modulation. However, bridging the gap between benchtop discovery and clinical application requires addressing two pivotal factors: standardized production and pharmacokinetic (PK) translation. The practical acquisition of CK has historically been a bottleneck due to its scarcity in raw ginseng. The shift toward enzymatic biocatalysis and microbial transformation, as detailed in this review, ensures a scalable and high-purity supply. These biotechnological advancements provide the necessary chemical standardization (CMC) required for rigorous clinical evaluation, overcoming the limitations of traditional extraction. It demonstrates superior membrane permeability and a multi-target pharmacological profile in comparison to its parent compounds. A pivotal mechanism elucidated in this review is CK’s sophisticated modulation of the Nrf2 signaling pathway, the master regulator of cellular redox homeostasis. CK has been identified as a robust upstream signaling tuner. It has been demonstrated to promote Nrf2 nuclear translocation and the subsequent activation of the Antioxidant Response Element (ARE), thereby orchestrating the transcription of a comprehensive suite of Phase II antioxidant enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 ( HO-1 ), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and glutathione peroxidase (GPx). The therapeutic relevance of this pathway is underscored by its ability to bridge the “concentration gap” between effective in vitro concentrations (5–50 μM) and the lower peak plasma levels (∼0.11–0.16 μM) typically

The CK-induced upregulation of HO-1 , in particular, has been demonstrated to mediate potent anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting microglial activation. The efficacy of CK in suppressing the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically IL-1β and TNF-α, is attributable to its ability to reinforce the Nrf2 -ARE- HO-1 axis. This, in turn, results in the interruption of the cycle of neuroinflammation and the preservation of neuronal integrity. Furthermore, this pathway provides sustained defense by generating protective metabolites, such as carbon monoxide and biliverdin, which synergistically mitigate mitochondrial ROS (mROS) generation and prevent the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) during acute ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury. title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: ABSTRACT Background Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of acute respiratory infection (ARI) in adults, especially older individuals, yet data on burden in Thailand are limited. This study aimed to describe clinical characteristics and mortality risk factors of RSV‐related hospitalizations in Thai adults. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis using Thailand's national hospital database, including adults aged ≥ 18 years hospitalized with RSV‐associated ARIs between June 2016 and September 2024, identified using ICD‐10 codes J12.1, J20.5, J21.0, and B97.4. Demographics, case fatality ratio, and healthcare resource utilization were assessed. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of in‐hospital mortality, and Kaplan–Meier analysis estimated 60‐day overall survival by age and comorbidity status. Results Among 1595 RSV‐related hospitalizations, the mean age was 66.5 years; 72.0% were aged ≥60 years and 78.4% had ≥ 1 comorbidity, most commonly

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: Results Among 1595 RSV‐related hospitalizations, the mean age was 66.5 years; 72.0% were aged ≥60 years and 78.4% had ≥ 1 comorbidity, most commonly hypertension, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, and chronic heart disease. The median length of stay (LOS) was 7 days, 17.3% required oxygen therapy, and 8.2% received invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV). The in‐hospital mortality was 9.53%. Mortality was independently associated with age ≥ 75 years (mOR 1.83, p = 0.019), LOS ≥ 7 days (1.95, p = 0.001), IMV (2.94, p < 0.001), pneumonia (4.10, p < 0.001), and acute myocardial infarction (3.05, p = 0.005). The 60‐day survival rate was 88.2%, declining to 84.0% in patients aged ≥ 75 years ( p < 0.001) and 87.1% in those with comorbidities versus 92.2% in those without ( p = 0.013). text: 4 Discussion This nationwide study is the first to comprehensively describe the burden, outcomes, and risk factors associated with RSV‐related hospitalizations among adults in Thailand using national data. Over an eight‐year period, 1595 unique admissions were analyzed. These findings demonstrate that RSV is an important cause of severe illness and death in adults. More than two‐thirds of patients were aged ≥ 60 years, 78% had comorbidities, and the in‐hospital CFR was 9.5%. These observations are consistent with global estimates of RSV‐related mortality ranging from 6 to 15% among hospitalized older adults [ 1 , 2 , 15 ], emphasizing that RSV poses a substantial health burden beyond pediatric populations. Compared with previous Thai studies by Chuaychoo et al. (2019) and Wongsurakiat et al. (2022), which focused on RSV cases in tertiary hospitals [ 11 , 12 ], our dataset captures broader demographic and geographic variation. Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic respiratory

text: hospitals [ 11 , 12 ], our dataset captures broader demographic and geographic variation. Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic respiratory disease, and chronic heart disease were the most frequent comorbidities, while 61.88% of patients had multimorbidity. HCRU was considerable: the median LOS was 7 days; more than half of patients were hospitalized for ≥ 7 days; 17% required oxygen therapy, and 8% required IMV. Patients with chronic heart disease and malignancy had prolonged hospitalizations (median LOS of 10 and 13 days, respectively). Adj RW were highest among patients aged ≥ 75 years (1.90), those with stroke (3.74), and those with malignancy (3.95), reflecting both clinical severity and economic burden. These findings are consistent with reports from South Korea and China, where RSV infection in older adults was associated with prolonged hospital stays, increased intensive care unit utilization, and higher healthcare costs [ 6 ]. A marked increase in RSV hospitalizations was

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: prolonged hospital stays, increased intensive care unit utilization, and higher healthcare costs [ 6 ]. A marked increase in RSV hospitalizations was observed in 2023, with a 5.3‐fold rise compared with the preceding year. Similar rebounds have been reported in many countries after relaxation of COVID‐19 control measures, likely related to reduced population exposure during the pandemic and the subsequent return of transmission [ 16 , 17 ]. In our data, however, hospitalization numbers remained elevated beyond the initial surge. Before COVID‐19, RSV testing in Thailand was available but was usually performed only in hospitalized patients with severe illness and mainly in children; routine testing in adults was uncommon. After the pandemic, many hospitals began using rapid antigen combination assays and multiplex RT‐PCR respiratory panels for patients admitted with acute respiratory illness, and RSV was incorporated into global respiratory surveillance programs [ 18 ]. These changes

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: for patients admitted with acute respiratory illness, and RSV was incorporated into global respiratory surveillance programs [ 18 ]. These changes likely increased recognition and laboratory confirmation of RSV infection in adults. Therefore, the sustained post‐pandemic rise in identified hospitalizations probably reflects both a temporary epidemiologic rebound and improved case detection rather than a true abrupt increase in disease incidence. Admissions also followed the expected seasonal pattern for tropical settings, occurring mainly in the latter half of the year and peaking between July and January, particularly in September and October [ 8 , 19 ]. In‐hospital mortality was driven by advanced age and comorbidity. Age ≥ 75 years and ≥ 1 comorbidity (particularly chronic heart disease, stroke, and malignancy) were significant predictors, as were pneumonia, AMI, prolonged LOS, and IMV. These findings corroborate previous Thai studies reporting high RSV‐related mortality among

text: as were pneumonia, AMI, prolonged LOS, and IMV. These findings corroborate previous Thai studies reporting high RSV‐related mortality among adults, ranging from 7.4% to 15.9% [ 11 , 12 ], and are consistent with global cohorts identifying cardiopulmonary comorbidities and severe complications as key risk factors [ 6 ]. However, the lower CFR observed in Thailand compared with other low‐ to middle‐income countries where RSV‐related CFRs reach up to 15.2% in high‐risk adults and 27.0% in adults aged > 60 years may reflect differences in healthcare system capacity, as Thailand's universal health coverage and access to hospital‐based care are more closely aligned with high‐income country settings [ 3 ]. Moreover, regional data from Malaysia similarly demonstrate age‐related increases in RSV hospitalization and mortality, particularly among adults aged ≥ 75 years [ 20 ]. Survival analysis elucidated the interaction between age and comorbidity. Overall, 60‐day survival was 88.2% and was

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: adults aged ≥ 75 years [ 20 ]. Survival analysis elucidated the interaction between age and comorbidity. Overall, 60‐day survival was 88.2% and was significantly lower among adults aged ≥ 75 years (84.0%) than among younger adults (92.8%), as well as among patients with comorbidities compared with those without (87.1% vs. 92.2%). The highest in‐hospital mortality was observed in adults aged ≥ 75 years with high‐risk comorbidities, particularly stroke, malignancy, and chronic heart disease. Collectively, these findings indicate that advanced age and comorbidity function as both independent and synergistic risk factors, identifying elderly adults with chronic disease as the most vulnerable subgroup. This pattern is consistent with prior studies demonstrating increased RSV hospitalization, severe disease, mortality, and healthcare resource utilization among older adults and those with cardiopulmonary or immunocompromised conditions [ 8 , 21 ], underscoring the importance of early

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: utilization among older adults and those with cardiopulmonary or immunocompromised conditions [ 8 , 21 ], underscoring the importance of early recognition and appropriate supportive care. Accordingly, adults aged ≥ 75 years and those with major comorbidities should be prioritized for preventive strategies and closer clinical monitoring. Recently, three RSV vaccines have been licensed for use in adults and have demonstrated efficacy in preventing RSV‐associated lower respiratory tract disease [ 22 , 23 , 24 ]. The adjuvanted RSV vaccine demonstrated durable protection against RSV‐related lower respiratory tract disease, such as pneumonia and severe RSV disease, in older adults aged ≥ 60 years, especially those with comorbidities, for at least three consecutive seasons [ 25 ]. Emerging real‐world data further support its importance, demonstrating high effectiveness in preventing RSV‐related hospitalizations (79% [95% CI 72–85]) in adults aged ≥ 60 years [ 26 , 27 , 28 ]. These findings

text: high effectiveness in preventing RSV‐related hospitalizations (79% [95% CI 72–85]) in adults aged ≥ 60 years [ 26 , 27 , 28 ]. These findings generated here may also be applicable to countries in Southeast Asia and other tropical or low‐ and middle‐income settings with similar demographic and health system characteristics. These findings support the consideration of prevention strategies tailored not only to Thailand's adult population and healthcare capacity but also to neighboring countries within the region. Notably, RSV vaccination in Thai adults aged ≥ 60 years has the potential to substantially reduce cases of ARI hospitalizations, pneumonia, and deaths [ 10 ]. The major strength of this study is the use of nationwide hospital data, which enabled a comprehensive and representative assessment of RSV hospitalizations in adults. This large dataset provides representative estimates of disease burden, HCRU, mortality risk factors, and survival outcomes. However, several limitations

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: large dataset provides representative estimates of disease burden, HCRU, mortality risk factors, and survival outcomes. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, hospitalization identification was based on ICD‐10 discharge diagnoses recorded in the National Health Security office (NHSO) reimbursement database, which undergoes administrative audit and verification. However, individual laboratory results were not available; therefore, some misclassification between pneumonia, bronchitis, and bronchiolitis may have occurred. In adults, cases coded as bronchitis or bronchiolitis likely reflected clinically significant lower respiratory tract infection requiring hospitalization, and this is unlikely to materially affect overall burden estimates. Second, detailed clinical variables, including immunization history, socioeconomic status, and functional status, were unavailable in the NHSO inpatient database. Third, immunocompromised conditions could not be comprehensively

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Hospitalizations Among Adults in Thailand: A Nationwide Retrospective Observational Study (RSV‐HAT)
text: status, and functional status, were unavailable in the NHSO inpatient database. Third, immunocompromised conditions could not be comprehensively identified using diagnosis codes alone, and treatment‐related immunosuppression may have been under‐ascertained; only solid organ transplantation was reliably captured as a high‐risk condition. Fourth, cost estimates based on Adj RW represent payer reimbursement and do not reflect hospital or societal costs. Finally, RSV cases are likely underreported due to limited routine RSV testing; in this context, a public health impact model may help better estimate the true disease burden and the potential population‐level benefits of vaccination beyond laboratory‐confirmed cases [ 10 ]. Despite these limitations, this study constitutes the largest and most representative analysis of adult RSV hospitalizations in Thailand to date.

5 Conclusion RSV is an important cause of hospitalization and death among Thai adults, with the highest risks observed among those aged ≥ 75 years and in patients with comorbidities. These populations experience prolonged hospital stays, increased need for critical care, and lower survival, underscoring their vulnerability. This study provides essential baseline evidence on the characteristics, HCRU, and outcomes of adult RSV hospitalizations in Thailand. The findings identify clear priority groups for prevention and clinical management and support health system preparedness, including evaluation of adult RSV vaccination strategies.

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: Patient: Female, 73-year-old Final Diagnosis: Heyde syndrome Symptoms: Fatigue • melena Clinical Procedure: EGD • TAVR Specialty: Cardiology • Gastroenterology and Hepatology • Hematology Objective: Unusual clinical course Background Heyde syndrome (HS) is defined by the triad of aortic stenosis (AS), gastrointestinal bleeding, and acquired von Willebrand syndrome (avWS). Diagnosis can be challenging in elderly patients with multiple comorbidities, particularly when angiodysplasia is absent on endoscopy. We present a case illustrating the diagnostic process and therapeutic outcome, emphasizing that the absence of angiodysplasia should not exclude HS. Case Report A 73-year-old woman with a history of AS, coronary artery disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and anemia presented with 2 weeks of melena and 1 week of fatigue. She was pale on exam with a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, microcytosis, and elevated troponin

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: on exam with a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. Laboratory evaluation showed hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL, microcytosis, and elevated troponin consistent with type II myocardial infarction due to demand ischemia. Prior endoscopic evaluations, including esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, and capsule studies, revealed melena but no bleeding source. Coagulation studies assessing von Willebrand factor activity were not available from the referring facility in this case. Transthoracic echocardiogram and cardiac catheterization confirmed severe AS (aortic valve area 0.4–0.7 cm 2 ) with concomitant coronary artery disease. The patient underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). At 6-month follow-up, she was asymptomatic, with resolution of anemia (hemoglobin 14 g/dL) and negative fecal occult blood testing. Conclusions Acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency diagnostic measures were unable to be provided from the facility at which she was originally admitted. This

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: Acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency diagnostic measures were unable to be provided from the facility at which she was originally admitted. This case underscores the importance of considering HS in patients with severe AS and recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding even when angiodysplasia is not visualized. Hemodynamic shear stress in AS leads to degradation of high-molecular-weight von Willebrand factor multimers, predisposing to bleeding. The resolution of anemia and bleeding after TAVR strongly supports the diagnosis. Early recognition and valve replacement are essential for effective management.

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: Discussion In HS, hemodynamic stress from AS leads to the breakdown of Hmw vWF multimers, impairing coagulation. This deficiency, combined with the presence of blood vessels, increases the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding. Underreporting suggests gaps in diagnosing and managing HS due to under-recognition of acquired von Willebrand syndrome (avWS) and the often intermittent nature of gastrointestinal bleeding. Although most published case reports describe discrete angiodysplasias, a systematic review of 77 case reports found that approximately 13% had no identifiable bleeding source despite multimodal endoscopic evaluation [ 2 ]. The absence of angiodysplasia does not rule out a potential diagnosis of Heyde syndrome, especially when the clinical picture aligns with the syndrome’s diagnostic triad. In our patient, no angiodysplasia was identified and avWS testing was not obtained, which is a gap in diagnostic workup that would disqualify Heyde syndrome as a potential diagnosis under a

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: and avWS testing was not obtained, which is a gap in diagnostic workup that would disqualify Heyde syndrome as a potential diagnosis under a more traditional framework. However, the patient’s complete cessation of bleeding after TAVR was consistent with rapid restoration of von Willebrand multimers, suggesting that a pattern of refractory bleeding that resolves promptly after valve intervention should strongly indicate Heyde syndrome, even in settings where avWS assays are unavailable. Other case reports in the literature corroborate the cessation of gastrointestinal bleeding after aortic valve intervention. Tsuchiya et al reported an 83-year-old woman with severe AS and gastric angiodysplasia in whom TAVI led to immediate recovery of HMW vWF multimers, disappearance of bleeding within 10 days, and complete endoscopic resolution of angiodysplasia by 4 months, with freedom from recurrent lesions or anemia at 2-year follow-up [ 6 ]. Lourdusamy et al, in their review, similarly collated

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: by 4 months, with freedom from recurrent lesions or anemia at 2-year follow-up [ 6 ]. Lourdusamy et al, in their review, similarly collated numerous case reports and series that observed the resolution of gastrointestinal bleeding in the context of aortic stenosis after valve replacement [ 7 ]. Clinical results strongly support the interpretation that in each of these cases AS-related acquired vWF defects were present but unmeasured, placing our patient within the clinical spectrum of Heyde syndrome despite the absence of documented angiodysplasia or definitive hematologic confirmation. Based on this case and review of the available literature, we propose a structured diagnostic and procedural algorithm to aid clinicians managing similar patients ( Figure 5 ). Procedural steps Diagnostic algorithm: • Diagnostic steps [ 8 ]: – Obtain medical history with inquiry of bleeding episodes, chronology of symptomatology, and medication use (i.e., anticoagulants). Assess for comorbidities

text: medical history with inquiry of bleeding episodes, chronology of symptomatology, and medication use (i.e., anticoagulants). Assess for comorbidities including CAD. – Perform a physical examination looking for signs of anemia and AS murmur. – Initial Investigations: • Complete blood count (CBC) evaluating for anemia and platelet count. • Coagulation profile: PT, aPTT, and INR for coagulation status. Use multimer analysis to determine vWF activity, low levels support diagnosis. • Echocardiogram to assess level of AS. – Investigating angiodysplasia: • Diagnosing intestinal angiodysplasia, often the underlying mechanism for Gastrointestinal bleeding, involves a stepwise approach utilizing various endoscopic techniques. How each technique contributes to the diagnostic process: – Colonoscopy, the initial step for evaluating the colon and distal parts of the small intestine, provides direct visualization of mucosal abnormalities (focal erythema, vascular lesions, or active bleeding sites).

text: parts of the small intestine, provides direct visualization of mucosal abnormalities (focal erythema, vascular lesions, or active bleeding sites). It enables biopsy of lesions for histopathological confirmation. – EGD examines the Gastrointestinal tract, detecting angiodysplasia and allowing for biopsy of lesions. – VCE provides a non-invasive visualization of the entire small bowel to detect lesions, including areas inaccessible by traditional endoscopy. This technique cannot biopsy or treat lesions identified. – DBE, an advanced endoscopic technique for deep small bowel exploration, enables visualization, therapeutic intervention (i.e, cautery or clipping of identified arteriovenous malformations [AVMs]), and biopsy throughout the small bowel. However, lesions may not always be identified if not actively bleeding. • If initial evaluation for intestinal angiodysplasia/AVMs is negative, proceed to VCE for small bowel evaluation. If uncertainty remains, use DBE for targeted

text: evaluation for intestinal angiodysplasia/AVMs is negative, proceed to VCE for small bowel evaluation. If uncertainty remains, use DBE for targeted intervention and biopsy. – Endoscopy: Indications: Gastrointestinal bleeding in HS. In our patient, gastrointestinal bleeding manifested as melena, anemia, and fatigue. Other indications are persistent or unexplained anemia despite treatment, abdominal pain, and change in bowel habits. • Procedure: 1. Pre-procedural preparation of patients includes fasting, consent, and anesthesia. 2. During the procedure, the endoscope is inserted through natural openings, such as the mouth or anus. 3. Images transmitted via the camera for visualization and examination allow for biopsies and interventions, including cauterization or removal of foreign bodies. TAVR procedure [ 8 ]: • Pre-procedural: – Evaluation: Thorough evaluation of the patient’s health, comorbidities, and suitability for a catheter-based procedure is conducted, including assessment of

text: Thorough evaluation of the patient’s health, comorbidities, and suitability for a catheter-based procedure is conducted, including assessment of bleeding risk using vWF levels, function, and specialized coagulation tests. – Anticoagulation: Thrombotic risk assessment guides antithrombotic therapy. – Imaging: Echocardiography, CT scan, or MRI can assess the anatomy of the AV, size of the annulus, and condition of the surrounding structures. • Procedure: 1. Intra-procedural monitoring and management: To minimize vascular trauma and bleeding, optimal vascular access strategy should be planned. 2. Anesthesia: Local anesthesia with conscious sedation is commonly used. 3. Access Site: Access through a large artery, such as the femoral artery, depending on the patient’s anatomy and individual factors. 4. Valve Deployment: A catheter with the collapsible replacement valve is guided through the access site and artery to the heart under imaging guidance. The new valve is expanded once properly

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: replacement valve is guided through the access site and artery to the heart under imaging guidance. The new valve is expanded once properly positioned within the native aortic valve, pushing the old valve leaflets out of the way, allowing the new valve to regulate blood flow. 5. Adjustment: Using echocardiography and angiography, the position and function of the new valve are assessed to ensure proper placement prior to closure. 6. Closure: Catheters are then removed, and the access site is closed using manual compression or a closure device. • Post-procedure: –Inpatient: Post-TAVR patients should be closely monitored for bleeding, arrhythmias, or vascular injury in cardiac intensive care unit. Rapid improvement allows for discharge within days if hemostasis is well-managed. – Outpatient: Cardiologist follow-ups to monitor prosthetic valve function and manage cardiac issues post-TAVR and long-term antithrombotic therapy should be individualized for patients. Potential pitfalls Drawbacks in this diagnostic algorithm include under-recognizing and inadequate screening of avWS, delayed AS diagnosis, misinterpreting gastrointestinal bleeding, and diminished interdisciplinary teamwork. Patients with unexplained bleeding should undergo thorough evaluation for the triad of HS, especially in elderly patients. Although TAVR is a generally safe and effective procedure for severe AS, potential complications include vascular injury, bleeding, valve issues (migration, malposition, embolization), new arrhythmias, stroke, kidney injury, and infection. Adhering carefully to diagnostic and procedural steps helps reduce risks.

title: An Uncommon Presentation of Heyde Syndrome: Absence of Visible Endoscopic Angiodysplasia With Resolution After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
text: Conclusions Although commonly linked to gastrointestinal bleeding, a recent study of 91 cases found that 20.5% did not exhibit angiodysplasia, challenging the traditional diagnostic criteria [ 9 ]. Therefore, the absence of angiodysplasia should not preclude a diagnosis of Heyde syndrome.

title: Environmental Exposures and Atherosclerotic Risk Factors in Vulnerable Youth: The Example of American Indian/Alaska Native Populations
text: Purpose of Review Environmental exposures are drivers of cardiovascular disease. These exposures, including climate change, metal toxicants, microplastics, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and particulate matter, can be inhaled, ingested, or absorbed through water or soil, and can promote atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, dysglycemia, and obesity. This review aims to describe environmental contributors to the development of ASCVD risk factors in childhood, with a focus on American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) children as a lens for exploring the linkage between marginalization and toxic exposures. Recent Finding Recent evidence suggests alarming associations between microplastics, endocrine-disrupting chemicals and ASCVD. Exposure to air pollution has also been demonstrated to increase the risk of ASCVD primarily through oxidative stress. Further, climate change impacts cardiovascular health by increasing metabolic demand and

title: Environmental Exposures and Atherosclerotic Risk Factors in Vulnerable Youth: The Example of American Indian/Alaska Native Populations
text: the risk of ASCVD primarily through oxidative stress. Further, climate change impacts cardiovascular health by increasing metabolic demand and disrupting economic supply chains and healthcare delivery. Toxic metal exposures also promote ASCVD through oxidative stress, inflammation, and endothelial dysfunction. Historically marginalized populations bear a disproportionate burden of these exposures, with AI/AN people as an illustrative example. ASCVD remains the most common cause of death in AI/AN people, and data describe an accelerated phenotype. This is likely in part attributable to inequitable environmental exposures driven by settler colonialism-influenced policies and land allocation patterns. Summary Emerging evidence suggests a need for research on the role of environmental exposure prevention in reducing ASCVD risk. Providers must screen for environmental contributors to ASCVD and partner with community resources, tribal communities, and state and federal surveillance efforts

title: Environmental Exposures and Atherosclerotic Risk Factors in Vulnerable Youth: The Example of American Indian/Alaska Native Populations
text: screen for environmental contributors to ASCVD and partner with community resources, tribal communities, and state and federal surveillance efforts to promote the cardiovascular health of all children.

title: Environmental Exposures and Atherosclerotic Risk Factors in Vulnerable Youth: The Example of American Indian/Alaska Native Populations
text: Discussion Emerging evidence supports an association between multiple environmental exposures and ASCVD risk factors and events. The most vulnerable children, including AI/AN youth, bear an inequitable burden of exposure that may worsen a higher prevalence and earlier onset of ASCVD phenotype. However, this review is limited by the observational design of the majority of included studies. Further research is needed into environmental exposures and ASCVD risk, particularly among younger participants. Fortunately, AI/AN communities have prioritized children's health, and many interventions have been developed and implemented to improve cardiovascular health [ 17 ]. Strengths-based, culturally-centered programming has demonstrated efficacy in promoting healthy dietary choices, physical activity, and cultural connectedness [ 17 ]. Further, increasing the utilization of traditional ecological knowledge, the cultural understanding of observed patterns inherited by Indigenous people from

title: Environmental Exposures and Atherosclerotic Risk Factors in Vulnerable Youth: The Example of American Indian/Alaska Native Populations
text: increasing the utilization of traditional ecological knowledge, the cultural understanding of observed patterns inherited by Indigenous people from their ancestors, serves as a means to address climate change and build relationships between communities and governments [ 118 ]. Data on selected environmental exposures underscore the importance of incorporating environmental health curricula into interventions tailored to AI/AN youth. Again, this has already been recognized as a priority by AI/AN communities [ 119 ]. Numerous programs exist to develop knowledge and leadership in environmental science and leadership, designed explicitly for AI/AN youth [ 119 ]. Given the inequities documented in the literature review and the significant ASCVD consequences, empowering the next generation of AI/AN leaders in the climate movement ultimately mitigates these risks for AI/AN children. Redressing the environmental degradation resulting from structural policy choices imposed on AI/AN populations

title: Environmental Exposures and Atherosclerotic Risk Factors in Vulnerable Youth: The Example of American Indian/Alaska Native Populations
text: these risks for AI/AN children. Redressing the environmental degradation resulting from structural policy choices imposed on AI/AN populations could include specific policy actions to mitigate environmental exposures, such as alternative fuel sources, innovative food provision programs, and direct healthcare targeting ASCVD risk factors across the life course. These actions could restore environmental justice and reduce ASCVD-related health consequences and societal costs. These strategies may serve as examples for other minoritized subgroups.

title: Environmental Exposures and Atherosclerotic Risk Factors in Vulnerable Youth: The Example of American Indian/Alaska Native Populations
text: Conclusions and Future Directions The evidence reveals that multiple environmental exposures impact the development of ASCVD in youth and minority communities, who may be at the greatest risk, as evidenced by the example of AI/AN children. Ultimately, adequately addressing environmental exposures in children, particularly AI/AN youth, requires communication and collaboration between providers, health systems, tribal governments, and communities. This includes leveraging individual clinical interactions to screen for these unique social drivers of health, identifying community resources, understanding available programming, and promoting cardiovascular health in the community [ 17 , 120 ]. Furthermore, international collaboration to understand environmental health concerns affecting global Indigenous communities and to develop strategies to mitigate their impacts improves the health of youth worldwide.

title: Real-world prevalence and outcome of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure in myelofibrosis
text: Background Myelofibrosis (MF) is a subgroup of Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms that are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, including pulmonary hypertension. Here we report the real-world prevalence, risk factors, and clinical outcomes of eRVSP in MF patients. Methods A retrospective, single-center cohort study was conducted on 208 patients with MF that were diagnosed between 2013 and 2023. Elevated right ventricular systolic pressure (eRVSP) was defined as RVSP > 35 mmHg. Major adverse cardiac events (MACE) were defined as new-onset congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease requiring intervention, cerebrovascular events, or cardiovascular death after MF diagnosis. Univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazard ratio regression model with eRVSP status as time-dependent covariate was used to estimate overall survival. Results Echocardiograms were performed in 208 MF patients, with RVSP estimates available in 156

title: Real-world prevalence and outcome of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure in myelofibrosis
text: covariate was used to estimate overall survival. Results Echocardiograms were performed in 208 MF patients, with RVSP estimates available in 156 patients (75%). eRVSP was present in 61 patients (39.1%). Patients with eRVSP were older (65 vs. 62 years, p = 0.053) and had higher rates of baseline hypertension (65.6% vs. 43.2%, p = 0.01), atrial fibrillation (16.4% vs. 4.2%, p = 0.02). MACE after diagnosis of MF occurred in 43 (20.7%) patients and was more frequent in eRVSP patients (36.1% vs. 15.8% p = 0.007), and this was predominantly driven by increased rates of new-onset congestive heart failure (27.9% vs. 8.4%, p = 0.003). In multivariable analysis, the presence of time-dependent eRVSP was associated with reduced survival (aHR: 4.41; 95%CI:2.84–6.85) after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates. Conclusions eRVSP was prevalent among MF patients undergoing echocardiogram and this was associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity, particularly HF. Furthermore, eRVSP was

text: among MF patients undergoing echocardiogram and this was associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity, particularly HF. Furthermore, eRVSP was associated with inferior survival and underscores the need for targeted screening and management in MF patients with cardiovascular risk factors and diseases. Prospective studies with baseline cardiovascular assessment and echocardiograms in all MF patients will establish true prevalence and may further elucidate the morbidity and mortality implication of eRVSP in MF patients. title: Real-world prevalence and outcome of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure in myelofibrosis
text: METHODS This was a retrospective, single-center cohort study of patients with a diagnosis of MF with echocardiogram who presented to Moffitt Cancer Center from 2013 to 2023. This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Moffitt Cancer Center (MCC18864). We retrospectively reviewed baseline CV comorbidities at the time of diagnosis or when first seen at our institution. CVD at baseline was defined as heart failure, coronary artery disease or stroke. Major adverse cardiac event (MACE) was defined as a new development of CHF, CAD requiring intervention, or stroke following diagnosis of MF. New-onset heart failure was defined as a clinical syndrome characterized by the inability of the heart to pump blood at an adequate volume to meet tissue metabolic requirements, or the ability to do so only at an elevation in the filling pressure diagnosed with an echocardiogram with structural and/or functional cardiac abnormality (systolic dysfunction with LVEF < 49%, or LVEF > 50% with

Acute coronary syndrome was defined as myocardial infarction or unstable angina with evidence of coronary artery disease on invasive or non-invasive testing. Stroke or TIA was defined as an episode of neurological dysfunction caused by infarction based on pathological, imaging, or other objective evidence of ischemic injury in a defined vascular distribution. text: RESULTS Within the 208 MF patients who had an echocardiogram performed, 156 patients (75%) had an echocardiogram with calculable RVSP estimates (Tables 1 and Supplemental Table 1). title: Real-world prevalence and outcome of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure in myelofibrosis
text: DISCUSSION In our MF cohort that underwent echocardiogram, the prevalence of eRVSP was relatively high at 39.1%. eRVSP was associated with systemic hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and older age [ 4 ]. Interestingly, factors with possible pathophysiologic links for eRVSP, such as JAK2 inhibitor use, transfusion dependency, or VTE were not associated with eRVSP. Overall, these findings indicate that the presence of risk factors for left heart disease is associated with eRVSP in patients with MF, and echocardiogram evaluation may be warranted in MF patients with cardiovascular risk factors. As only a subset of MF patients underwent echocardiogram, we hypothesized overestimation of eRVSP prevalence may occur. However, the weighted prevalence of eRVSP increased to 48.4%. This paradoxical finding is likely from selection process for echocardiogram. Patients planned for allogeneic SCT over-represent those undergoing echocardiogram (45%) and have lower eRVSP prevalence. SCT candidates are

title: Real-world prevalence and outcome of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure in myelofibrosis
text: Patients planned for allogeneic SCT over-represent those undergoing echocardiogram (45%) and have lower eRVSP prevalence. SCT candidates are likely healthier and less likely to have baseline cardiovascular disease. Therefore, the IPW-adjustment appropriately down-weights this overrepresented population, revealing a higher prevalence of eRVSP in general MF population. Our real-world evidence suggests that routine baseline echocardiogram may be considered for all MF patients, particularly in those not considered for SCT who may be systematically not undergo echocardiogram despite potentially higher eRVSP risk. Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminant potential (CHIP) is an age-related phenomenon and is associated various cardiovascular disease. In contrast to our initial hypothesis that the presence of CHIP-related mutation is associated with eRVSP, the presence of these mutations was not associated with eRVSP. Overall, these findings indicate there is no association between MF-driver or

title: Real-world prevalence and outcome of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure in myelofibrosis
text: eRVSP, the presence of these mutations was not associated with eRVSP. Overall, these findings indicate there is no association between MF-driver or common somatic CHIP-related mutations with eRVSP, suggesting that these mutations alone are not sufficient to drive eRVSP development. The interplay between these mutations and other eRVSP mechanisms, such as left-sided heart disease or non-CHIP mediated pro-inflammation, requires further investigation [ 6 ]. However, given the limited number of patients with CHIP-related mutations, the study is underpowered to show association between somatic mutations and adverse cardiovascular events. The presence of eRVSP was associated with increased MACE, most notably new onset CHF. Pathophysiologic links between eRVSP and CHF are well established, where eRVSP increases right ventricular afterload that leads to right-sided dysfunction and, in some cases, left-sided heart failure. Thus, as eRVSP is a marker of underlying cardiopulmonary pathology, its

title: Real-world prevalence and outcome of elevated right ventricular systolic pressure in myelofibrosis
text: to right-sided dysfunction and, in some cases, left-sided heart failure. Thus, as eRVSP is a marker of underlying cardiopulmonary pathology, its identification maybe important for risk stratification and prognostication in MF. However, it is also possible that as eRVSP is a marker for diastolic dysfunction, it is possible that subclinical or evolving CHF led to eRVSP, rather than eRVSP being a driver of HF. Future studies with serial echocardiograms and longitudinal clinical outcomes data would address these questions. Further, eRVSP as time-dependent covariate was independently associated with inferior survival. It is unclear whether eRVSP directly or indirectly contributes to increased mortality. The presence of eRVSP may have led to clinical decision not to pursue potentially cardiotoxic anti-cancer therapy. Regardless, the strong association of eRVSP with increased MACE and mortality underscores the need for systematic screening and targeted management in MF patients with an

There are several limitations to our study. First, there is selection bias, as we only investigated those MF patients who had an echocardiogram, not the whole cohort with MF. We do not have cardiovascular outcomes in those without an echocardiogram, as our study aim was to investigate the role of eRVSP in outcomes of myelofibrosis patients. To address this, we performed IPW analysis for the weighted prevalence of eRVSP. However, this should be interpreted cautiously, as we cannot directly verify eRVSP in those without echocardiogram. Also, 25% of patients without calculable RVSP due to insufficient TR jet usually have a lower chance of significant eRVSP and may overestimate the prevalence of eRVSP. Also, we have not stratified further with left-sided heart disease due to insufficient data. However, significant amount of patients underwent echocardiogram as a workup for allogeneic stem cell transplant evaluation. Third, the timing of echocardiograms for patients varied in relation to MF. To overcome immortality bias, we considered eRVSP status as time-dependent variable which allows an understanding of survival after diagnosis of eRVSP. text: CONCLUSIONS In conclusion, eRVSP was prevalent among MF patients undergoing echocardiogram and this was associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity, particularly HF. Furthermore, eRVSP was associated with inferior survival and underscores the need for targeted screening and management in MF patients with cardiovascular risk factors and diseases. Prospective studies with baseline cardiovascular assessment and echocardiograms in all MF patients will establish true prevalence and may further elucidate the morbidity and mortality implication of eRVSP in MF patients.
