text: 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design and Population This prospective cohort study included participants from the community‐dwelling population of the Shougang community in Shijingshan District, Beijing, China [ 18 ]. The parent cohort comprised 9540 residents aged ≥40 years who were recruited between December 2011 and April 2012 through community health center records, posters, or invitation calls. From this cohort, in 2014 (May to July), 5962 participants with available genetic data were invited for follow‐up, of whom 3881 (65.1%) responded and attended the survey (originally reported as 3823 [64.1%]; revised to 3881 [65.1%] after individual identity verification) [ 18 ]. As previously reported, baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between responders and non‐responders [ 18 ]. For the present analysis, we excluded participants with a history of stroke or myocardial infarction (MI), as well as those newly diagnosed with either condition in or before 2014. We further excluded

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: with a history of stroke or myocardial infarction (MI), as well as those newly diagnosed with either condition in or before 2014. We further excluded individuals with incomplete data on triglyceride (TG), fasting blood glucose (FBG), or WHtR in either the 2012 or 2014 surveys. Consequently, the final analytic sample consisted of 3466 participants (Figure S1 ). Prior to participation, all individuals were fully informed about the study procedures and provided written informed consent. The research protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of Peking University First Hospital. 2.2 Data Collection and Definitions Sociodemographic and medical history information was obtained through interviewer‐administered questionnaires conducted by trained personnel [ 18 ]. Participants were considered current smokers if their tobacco use amounted to at least one cigarette per day sustained more than six months. Current drinkers were defined as those consuming alcohol on one or more

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: amounted to at least one cigarette per day sustained more than six months. Current drinkers were defined as those consuming alcohol on one or more occasions per week for a minimum of six consecutive months. The body mass index (BMI) was determined by dividing an individual's weight in kilograms by their height in meters squared. Hypertension was identified based on a self‐reported diagnosis, SBP ≥140 mmHg, DBP ≥90 mmHg, or antihypertensive medication use. Diabetes mellitus was identified based on a self‐reported diagnosis, FBG ≥7.0 mmol/L, OGTT ≥11.1 mmol/L, or use of glucose‐lowering drugs. MAP was calculated as DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3. The change in MAP was calculated as the MAP at in 2014 minus that at 2012. After a 12‐hour fasting period, participants were required to fast overnight and then provide a venous blood sample from their forearm. The following biochemical parameters were assessed: FBG, lipids, and creatinine. A venous blood sample was collected two hours after a meal to

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: The following biochemical parameters were assessed: FBG, lipids, and creatinine. A venous blood sample was collected two hours after a meal to perform the standard 75 g OGTT for measuring two‒hour postprandial blood glucose. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was computed via the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD–EPI) equation [ 19 ] in the 2014 survey. Each of the experimental parameters was meticulously quantified using the Roche C8000 Automated Analytical System. 2.3 Evaluation of Changes in TyG–WHtR The TyG‒WHtR was determined using the formula as below [ 20 ] TyG − WHtR = ln TG mg / dL × FBG mg / dL 2 × waist circumference cm height cm The change in TyG‒WHtR was determined by subtracting the 2012 value from the 2014 measurement. 2.4 Outcomes and Follow‐up The follow‐up period extended from 2014 to December 31, 2021. Follow‐up time was calculated from baseline to the occurrence of the composite endpoint or the end of follow‐up. The total follow‐up

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: 31, 2021. Follow‐up time was calculated from baseline to the occurrence of the composite endpoint or the end of follow‐up. The total follow‐up duration was 24 930.71 person‐years, with a median of 7.52 years. During this period, only a subset of participants returned for on‐site physical and laboratory examinations in 2018, rather than the entire cohort. Therefore, the absolute change in TyG–WHtR values between 2012 and 2014 was used as the exposure variable, instead of a time‐dependent TyG–WHtR measure. The primary outcome was the occurrence of MACEs, defined as a composite of the first nonfatal stroke, the first nonfatal MI, or cardiovascular death during the follow‒up period. The secondary outcomes were the individual components of MACEs. For continuous variables, data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for normally distributed

text: were assessed using the chi‐square test. For continuous variables, data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) for normally distributed variables or as median (interquartile range, IQR) for non‐normally distributed variables, with comparisons made using the independent‐samples t‐test or the Mann–Whitney U test, respectively. To identify a potential threshold for the change in TyG‐WHtR, segmented (piece‐wise) Cox regression was performed. A significant threshold was determined by comparing the segmented model to a linear model using the log‐likelihood ratio test. The specific threshold value (inflection point) was selected as the point that maximized the model likelihood, identified via a two‐step recursive algorithm. This data‐derived threshold was then used for subsequent categorical analyses. To examine the relationship between the two‐year changes in TyG–WHtR and the outcomes, Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95%

text: the two‐year changes in TyG–WHtR and the outcomes, Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All models were adjusted for a comprehensive set of covariates: age, sex, current smoking, current alcohol consumption status, eGFR, history of hypertension, history of diabetes mellitus, HDL‐C, LDL‐C, and the use of antihypertensive, glucose‐lowering, and lipid‐lowering medications. To account for the potential influence of baseline levels, the baseline (2012) TyG–WHtR was also included as a covariate. The change in TyG‒WHtR was analyzed both as a continuous and as a categorical variable. Potential nonlinear relationships between changes in TyG–WHtR and MACEs were evaluated using restricted cubic spline (RCS) within the Cox proportional hazards model, with four knots and adjustment for all aforementioned covariates. Landmark analysis was conducted with the cut‒off point set at 2 years, based on the observed

text: knots and adjustment for all aforementioned covariates. Landmark analysis was conducted with the cut‒off point set at 2 years, based on the observed overlap and crossing of the Kaplan‒Meier curves. Separate Cox models were fitted for the periods 0‒2 years and >2 years. Furthermore, causal mediation analysis was conducted to investigate the possible mediating role of change in MAP on the relationship between change in TyG–WHtR and the risk of MACEs. Although Cox proportional hazards models were used for primary analyses, we note that estimating direct and indirect effects under the Cox framework relies on the rare‐event assumption [ 21 ]. In contrast, the accelerated failure time (AFT) model does not require this assumption and offers a more natural integration within mediation frameworks for time‐to‐event data [ 22 ]. Therefore, we primarily present the mediation results based on the AFT model in the main text, while also providing results from the proportional hazards model for

text: primarily present the mediation results based on the AFT model in the main text, while also providing results from the proportional hazards model for comparison, which were largely consistent. In the mediation analysis, first, a linear regression model was fitted with the change in MAP as the dependent variable, and the change in TyG‒WHtR along with all covariates as independent variables. Second, a parametric AFT model was fitted with MACEs‐free survival time as the outcome, and the change in TyG–WHtR along with either the change in MAP (plus MAP in 2012), the change in LDL‐C (plus LDL‐C in 2012), or the change in HDL‐C (plus HDL‐C in 2012)–together with all covariates–as independent variables. The proportional hazards assumption was examined using Schoenfeld residuals. Although the Kaplan–Meier curves appeared to overlap during the early follow‐up, the test indicated that the assumption was not violated for any covariates or for the overall model. text: follow‐up, the test indicated that the assumption was not violated for any covariates or for the overall model. E ‐values were also calculated for the HRs (point estimate and lower 95% CI bound) to evaluate sensitivity to potential unmeasured confounding. All analyses were performed using R programming language (version 4.3.2 and version 4.4.3; https://www.r‐project.org/ ). Two‐sided tests were applied, and a p ‐value <0.050 was regarded as statistically significant.

text: To further characterize this relationship, the change in TyG‒WHtR was dichotomized based on the identified threshold. Kaplan–Meier curves (Figure 1 ) demonstrated a significantly higher cumulative hazard for MACE in the ≥0.400 group compared to the <0.400 group (log‐rank p = 0.015, Figure 1A ). In the fully adjusted Cox model (Table 3 ), per SD increase in TyG‒WHtR as a continuous variable was associated with a 15% higher hazard of MACE (HR: 1.15 [1.02–1.30], p = 0.024), corresponding to an E ‐value of 1.57 for the point estimate (Table S8 ). John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. 3.5 Mediation Analysis of Concurrent Change in MAP To explore the potential pathways linking change in TyG–WHtR to future MACEs, we conducted mediation analyses with three candidate mediators: concurrent changes in MAP (Figure 3 ), LDL‐C (Table S2 ), and HDL‐C (Table S3 ). Only concurrent change in MAP showed a significant mediating effect (Figure 3 ) and the scatter plot of changes in TyG–WHtR and concurrent changes in MAP is presented in Figure S7 . As shown in Figure 3 , in model 1 (adjusted for demographics and laboratory values, but not clinical diagnoses or medications), the total effect of change in TyG‒WHtR on MACEs‒free survival time was significant (total effect estimate = −35.99, p = 0.020). The indirect effect mediated through changes in MAP was −9.86 ( p < 0.001), accounting for 27.4% of the total effect. After accounting for this mediation, the direct effect of change in TyG‒WHtR was attenuated and

In the fully adjusted model 2, the total effect remained significant (total effect estimate = −34.09, p = 0.034); the indirect effect via change in MAP was −10.37 ( p < 0.001), representing 30.4% of the total effect. The direct effect was again non‐significant (direct effect estimate = −23.71, p = 0.148), indicating that change in MAP explained a substantial portion of the association between change in TyG‒WHtR and MACEs risk. For comparison, we also performed the mediation analysis within the Cox proportional hazards model (Table S4 ). title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: 4 Discussion Evidence from this prospective study suggests that a two‐year increase in the TyG–WHtR index‒an integrated marker of IR and visceral adiposity‒is independently associated with future CVD risk. First, a two‐year increase of TyG‒WHtR of ≥0.400 was an independent predictor of higher incidence of MACE. Second, this relationship exhibits markedly nonlinearity, with cardiovascular risk rising sharply only after surpassing this potential threshold (≥0.400). Finally, approximately 30% of the association between the change in TyG‒WHtR and MACE risk appears to be mediated by concurrent change in MAP. In this study, a greater two‐year increase in the TyG‒WHtR‒ reflecting short‐term metabolic worsening‒ was associated with elevated long‑term cardiovascular risk. The prognostic strength of TyG‒WHtR likely stems from its dual representation of two core pathophysiological process: systemic IR and dysfunctional visceral adiposity [ 6 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 23 ]. First, the TyG index is a

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: of two core pathophysiological process: systemic IR and dysfunctional visceral adiposity [ 6 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 23 ]. First, the TyG index is a well‒validated and cost‒effective surrogate for IR, a foundational metabolic defect that promotes hyperglycemia, atherogenic dyslipidemia, and endothelial dysfunction [ 24 ]. Second, an elevated WHtR reflects increased visceral adipose tissue. This dysfunctional fat depot releases excess free fatty acids, reactive oxygen species, and pro‒inflammatory cytokines, leading to lipotoxicity and disruption of glucose homeostasis [ 25 , 26 , 27 ]. Consequently, composite indices like TyG‐WHtR, which integrate these synergistic pathways, have been shown to outperform either component alone in predicting cardiometabolic diseases and cardiovascular risk [ 15 , 16 , 20 , 28 , 29 , 30 ]. To our knowledge, few studies have investigated the prognostic value of fixed‐period changes in TyG–WHtR, which reflect short‐term metabolic worsening, for incident CVD.

text: studies have investigated the prognostic value of fixed‐period changes in TyG–WHtR, which reflect short‐term metabolic worsening, for incident CVD. A relevant investigation by Ren et al. [ 20 ] used data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) to identify three distinct TyG‒WHtR trajectory patterns between 2012 and 2015 via K‒means clustering. They reported that participants with moderate‒increasing or high‒slowly increasing trajectories had a higher CVD risk compared to those in a low‒stable pattern. However, their analysis focused on long‐term trajectory patterns rather than a defined short‐term change, and CVD outcomes were based on self‐report. In contrast, our study employed rigorously adjudicated hard endpoints from medical records to demonstrate that a greater two‐year increase in TyG–WHtR is independently associated with long‐term cardiovascular risk. This finding highlights the value of monitoring short‐term metabolic progression for early risk

text: associated with long‐term cardiovascular risk. This finding highlights the value of monitoring short‐term metabolic progression for early risk stratification. Change in TyG–WHtR is conceptually complementary to static risk scores such as China‐PAR [ 31 ]. In our joint stratification analysis (Figure S8 , Table S7 ), change in TyG–WHtR meaningfully refined risk among individuals classified as high risk by China‐PAR. By contrast, risk separation was not evident in the China‐PAR low‐risk group. These findings support change in TyG–WHtR as a simple longitudinal marker for monitoring metabolic deterioration and re‐stratifying risk beyond a single baseline estimate. Practically, it requires only fasting glucose, triglycerides, waist circumference, and height, facilitating repeated assessment in routine care and large‐scale or resource‐limited settings. Furthermore, our analysis provides insight into the determinants associated with an increase in TyG‐WHtR, particularly changes exceeding the

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: Furthermore, our analysis provides insight into the determinants associated with an increase in TyG‐WHtR, particularly changes exceeding the threshold of 0.400 over two years (Table S6 ). We identified that the presence of hypertension, current smoking, and an increase in LDL‐C was independently associated with greater TyG‐WHtR progression, whereas an increase in HDL‐C exerted a strong protective effect. These findings suggest that individuals with hypertension, high LDL‐C levels, low HDL‐C levels, or active smoking habits may be at heightened risk of accelerated IR deterioration, even in the absence of significant changes in traditional risk factors such as diabetes status. From a clinical perspective, monitoring these modifiable factors—especially through serial measurements of lipid profiles—could help identify patients who are progressing toward high metabolic‐cardiovascular risk earlier than would be possible using baseline data alone. Future studies should evaluate whether

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: toward high metabolic‐cardiovascular risk earlier than would be possible using baseline data alone. Future studies should evaluate whether interventions targeting these determinants (e.g., aggressive dyslipidemia management, or smoking cessation) can attenuate IR progression and ultimately improve cardiovascular outcomes. The association between a TyG–WHtR increase ≥0.400 and cardiovascular outcomes, including both the MACEs and the MI, appeared to strengthen and become statistically significant after approximately two years of follow‐up. This delayed emergence of statistical significance aligns with the known natural history of atherosclerosis, particularly in a primary cohort such as ours, which included only individuals without established CVD at baseline [ 32 , 33 ]. Atherosclerosis progresses through sequential stages, from initial endothelial dysfunction and lipid infiltration to the formation of a complex, unstable plaque prone to rupture [ 24 , 34 ]. A sharp rise in TyG‒WHtR,

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: endothelial dysfunction and lipid infiltration to the formation of a complex, unstable plaque prone to rupture [ 24 , 34 ]. A sharp rise in TyG‒WHtR, indicative of a worsening metabolic state characterized by IR and visceral adiposity, likely acts as a potent accelerator of this entire cascade by promoting chronic systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and atherogenic dyslipidemia, ultimately leading to clinical events [ 24 , 35 ]. However, it could also be influenced by the lower number of events occurring in the immediate years after baseline assessment, resulting in reduced statistical power to detect an early effect. Thus, the findings for both the MACE and the MI should be interpreted with caution and future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to confirm or refute this specific association. Building on mechanistic and longitudinal evidence supporting a biologically plausible link between worsening IR/central adiposity and blood pressure elevation [ 36 , 37 , 38

text: and longitudinal evidence supporting a biologically plausible link between worsening IR/central adiposity and blood pressure elevation [ 36 , 37 , 38 ], we evaluated concurrent change in MAP as a potential pathway in the association between two‐year change in TyG–WHtR and subsequent outcomes. Our mediation models suggested that approximately one‐third of the association between increasing TyG–WHtR and shorter MACEs‐free survival was statistically explained by concomitant increases in MAP. This finding aligns with the well‐established role of IR in the pathogenesis of hypertension. IR contributes to elevated blood pressure through multiple pathways [ 39 , 40 ]: by promoting sympathetic nervous system activation [ 41 ]; by enhancing renin‒angiotensin‒aldosterone system (RAAS) activity [ 42 , 43 , 44 ]; by inducing endothelial dysfunction through impaired nitric oxide‒mediated vasodilation [ 45 ]. These pathophysiological alterations collectively increase arterial stiffness and systemic

title: Dynamic Changes in Triglyceride Glucose‒Waist‒to‒Height Ratio and the Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events: Role of Concurrent Mean Arterial Pressure Change
text: impaired nitric oxide‒mediated vasodilation [ 45 ]. These pathophysiological alterations collectively increase arterial stiffness and systemic vascular resistance, resulting in a rise in MAP. In a related context, Xu et al. [ 46 ] reported that baseline TyG‒WHtR was associated with incident self‐reported CVD and more than 50% of this association was mediated by baseline MAP. Clinically, integrated strategies aimed at improving insulin sensitivity and reducing central obesity—together with optimal blood pressure management—may help mitigate hemodynamic burden and potentially lower downstream cardiovascular risk.

text: 6 Conclusion In this cohort study, a greater two‐year increase in TyG–WHtR was associated with a higher long‐term risk of MACEs. This association exhibited a nonlinear pattern, with cardiovascular risk accelerating sharply among individuals whose increase in TyG–WHtR exceeded a threshold, reflecting a state of short‐term metabolic worsening. Mediation analysis indicated that concurrent change in MAP explained approximately one‐third of this association, suggesting a significant hemodynamic pathway through which metabolic dysregulation may translate into elevated cardiovascular risk.

title: Association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and carotid plaque: a retrospective cohort study
text: Objective To investigate the association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (NHHR) and the risk of carotid plaque (CP). Methods In this cohort study, 5,985 adults aged ≥18 years without baseline CP were selected from the Dalian Health Management Cohort (2015–2023). Participants were categorized into quartiles according to NHHR levels. Kaplan–Meier curves were used to estimate cumulative CP incidence. Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses were applied to evaluate the association between NHHR and CP risk. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the findings. Results During 11,725.34 person-years of follow-up (mean follow-up: 2.24 years), 780 participants (13.03%) developed CP. Compared with participants in the lowest NHHR quartile, those in the highest quartile had a significantly increased risk of CP (HR = 1.64, 95% CI: 1.26–2.14; p < 0.001). When

title: Association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and carotid plaque: a retrospective cohort study
text: in the lowest NHHR quartile, those in the highest quartile had a significantly increased risk of CP (HR = 1.64, 95% CI: 1.26–2.14; p < 0.001). When treated as a continuous variable, NHHR remained independently associated with CP risk (HR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.04–1.18; p = 0.001). RCS analysis demonstrated a nonlinear positive association (P for nonlinearity = 0.003), with an inflection point at NHHR = 4.071. Significant interactions were observed for age, sex, and hypertension status (all P for interaction < 0.05), with stronger associations among individuals aged <45 years, females, and normotensive participants. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the results. Conclusion Elevated NHHR is independently associated with an increased risk of CP, with effect modification by age, sex, and hypertension status. NHHR may serve as a simple and noninvasive biomarker for early risk stratification of CP.

Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the findings, which remained consistent with the primary analysis ( Supplementary Table S7 ). The association between NHHR and CP persisted after excluding participants who developed CP within the first year of follow-up (HR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.30–2.39, p < 0.001), those with baseline hypertension, diabetes, or dyslipidemia (HR = 2.39, 95% CI: 1.54–3.71, p < 0.001), and those reporting medication use at baseline (HR = 1.79, 95% CI: 1.33–2.42, p < 0.001). Further adjustment for baseline cIMT did not materially change the results, with the highest NHHR quartile still associated with an increased risk of CP (HR = 1.67, 95% CI: 1.28–2.19, p < 0.001) ( Supplementary Table S8 ).

text: Discussion In this cohort, elevated NHHR was independently associated with higher CP risk. In fully adjusted models, participants in Q4 had a 1.64-fold higher risk of CP compared with those in Q1. RCS revealed a nonlinear positive association with an inflection at NHHR = 4.071; below this point, risk rose significantly with NHHR, while above this point, the NHHR-related risk of new-onset CP remained relatively stable. Subgroup analyses identified significant interactions of NHHR with age, sex, and hypertension status. Multiple sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness, supporting NHHR as an independent risk marker of CP. NHHR, as a novel composite biomarker for health risk assessment, integrates levels of pro-atherogenic lipoproteins and protective HDL-C, making it superior to traditional single lipid indicators in evaluating atherosclerosis risk ( 22 , 23 ). Recent research highlights NHHR’s enhanced performance in predicting cardiovascular events ( 24 , 25 ). For instance, the

title: Association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and carotid plaque: a retrospective cohort study
text: risk ( 22 , 23 ). Recent research highlights NHHR’s enhanced performance in predicting cardiovascular events ( 24 , 25 ). For instance, the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study demonstrated an independent association between NHHR and lipid cores in carotid plaques ( 26 ). Additional evidence corroborates NHHR’s close links to carotid atherosclerosis progression and plaque stability ( 27 , 28 ). Our findings align with these, showing that Q4 participants had a 1.64-fold higher CP risk than Q1, indicating a progressive increase in CP prevalence with rising NHHR levels ( 28 ). This is consistent with prior studies, such as that by Qin et al. ( 29 ), which reported a stepwise increase in cIMT across NHHR quartiles, collectively underscoring the strong connection between NHHR and CP risk. The restricted cubic spline analysis revealed a nonlinear positive correlation between NHHR and CP risk, with an identified inflection point at 4.071. Above this threshold, the risk increase

text: a nonlinear positive correlation between NHHR and CP risk, with an identified inflection point at 4.071. Above this threshold, the risk increase remained relatively stable. This pattern may be explained by the exclusion of participants with pre-existing CP at baseline, and the limited sample size at higher NHHR levels. Therefore, this finding requires validation in larger studies. In addition, the potential occurrence of cardiovascular events during follow-up may also influence the observed association, which warrants further investigation. Similar nonlinear relationships have also been reported between NHHR and other adverse metabolic outcomes ( 11 , 30 ). Notably, the threshold of NHHR varies across clinical outcomes: inflection points for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in adults with diabetes or prediabetes were 2.72 and 2.83 ( 31 ), respectively, whereas a threshold of 6.28 was identified for cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes ( 32 ). Previous

title: Association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and carotid plaque: a retrospective cohort study
text: 2.83 ( 31 ), respectively, whereas a threshold of 6.28 was identified for cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes ( 32 ). Previous subgroup analyses have indicated significant associations between NHHR and CP stability across strata of sex, age, hypertension, status ( 28 ). Our findings further demonstrated that NHHR was associated with higher hazard ratios in individuals aged <45 years, females, and those without hypertension. Possible explanations include: First, the cohort’s exclusion of high-risk individuals at baseline may amplify NHHR’s early warning value in relatively healthy populations. Second, younger adults often exhibit better lipid metabolic compensation, rendering early-stage atherosclerosis more sensitive to mild dyslipidemia ( 33 , 34 ), where inflammation and lipid abnormalities synergistically drive progression ( 35 ). Third, the stronger NHHR–CP association observed in females in our sex-stratified analysis may be associated with sex

title: Association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and carotid plaque: a retrospective cohort study
text: drive progression ( 35 ). Third, the stronger NHHR–CP association observed in females in our sex-stratified analysis may be associated with sex hormone-related differences in lipid metabolism, including the regulatory effects of estrogen on HDL functionality and LDL phenotypes ( 36 , 37 ). This echoes previous findings of a more pronounced NHHR-CP association in women ( 38 ). Finally, hypertension independently accelerates atherosclerosis, potentially diminishing NHHR’s relative predictive power in hypertensive individuals ( 39 ), leading to weaker risk differentiation. The underlying mechanisms by which NHHR promotes CP formation likely involve multiple pathways. Elevated NHHR signifies an increased burden of atherogenic lipoproteins coupled with diminished protective HDL-C function, collectively fostering endothelial dysfunction ( 40 ). Studies have linked higher NHHR to reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and elevated endothelin-1 (ET-1) levels ( 41 ). Inflammation plays a pivotal

title: Association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and carotid plaque: a retrospective cohort study
text: Studies have linked higher NHHR to reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and elevated endothelin-1 (ET-1) levels ( 41 ). Inflammation plays a pivotal role in this association, with NHHR elevation correlating to increased levels of inflammatory markers such as high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF- α ) ( 42 , 43 ). Oxidative stress represents another key mechanism, as high NHHR level is associated with elevated oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) and reduced antioxidant enzyme activity ( 44 ). Furthermore, NHHR’s interconnections with metabolic factors like obesity, hyperglycemia, and hypertension may exacerbate atherosclerosis progression ( 45 ). These mechanisms indirectly bolster our conclusions, affirming NHHR’s clinical utility in predicting CP risk. The strengths of this study include its use of large-scale cohort data to substantiate the association between NHHR and CP, reducing the likelihood of reverse

text: of this study include its use of large-scale cohort data to substantiate the association between NHHR and CP, reducing the likelihood of reverse causation. Comprehensive control for confounding was achieved through directed acyclic graphs, multiple modelling approaches, subgroup analyses, and sensitivity tests, all of which support the robustness of the findings. Notably, the heightened predictive efficacy of NHHR in younger, female, and non-hypertensive subgroups provides evidence-based guidance for precision screening in specific populations. During a mean follow-up of 2.24 years, 13.03% of participants developed CP. When both baseline cases ( n = 1,778) and incident cases ( n = 780) were considered within the initially screened population ( n = 9,679), the overall proportion of CP was broadly comparable in magnitude to the approximately 26% prevalence reported in recent studies in China, supporting the representativeness of our study population, although such comparisons should be

title: Association between the non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio and carotid plaque: a retrospective cohort study
text: 26% prevalence reported in recent studies in China, supporting the representativeness of our study population, although such comparisons should be interpreted cautiously. However, several limitations should be considered. Firstly, although NHHR was significantly associated with CP risk, its incremental predictive value was modest, and residual confounding from unmeasured or unknown factors cannot be entirely excluded, as some baseline variables were missing and medication use was not fully captured. Secondly, the study population was exclusively Chinese and derived from a routine health examination cohort, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other populations and necessitates external validation in diverse settings. Thirdly, CP was assessed using ultrasonography, which is operator-dependent and may be subject to interobserver bias despite standardized procedures. In addition, the lack of quantitative assessment of plaque morphology, stability, or phenotypic

text: interobserver bias despite standardized procedures. In addition, the lack of quantitative assessment of plaque morphology, stability, or phenotypic characteristics precludes a more detailed evaluation of the relationship between NHHR and plaque features. Future prospective studies with more comprehensive data collection and repeated measurements are warranted.

text: Conclusion NHHR is independently associated with the risk of CP. As an inexpensive and readily available biomarker derived from routine lipid testing, NHHR may assist in identifying individuals at elevated risk of CP. Further prospective studies are warranted to confirm its clinical relevance.

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: Objective Postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious complication following hip fracture surgery in older adults. This study aimed to identify predictors of postoperative AKI and evaluate its association with short-term complications after extracapsular hip fracture surgery. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted using TriNetX Analytics, a federated electronic health record network of 109 United States healthcare organizations (2015-2025). Adults aged ≥ 65 years undergoing extracapsular hip fracture surgery (CPT 27244/27245) were included; those with prior AKI (ICD-10-CM N17) were excluded. Propensity score matching was performed 1:1. Predictors were assessed using Cox proportional hazards modeling and postoperative complications were compared using risk ratios, odds ratios, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Results Among 46,287 eligible patients, 1,413 matched pairs (n=2,826) were analyzed. Predictors of postoperative AKI included Black race

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: analysis. Results Among 46,287 eligible patients, 1,413 matched pairs (n=2,826) were analyzed. Predictors of postoperative AKI included Black race (HR=1.64), White race (HR=1.21), elevated preoperative serum chloride (HR=1.04), bicarbonate (HR=1.03), creatinine (HR=1.18), and decreased serum protein (HR=1.11). Protective factors included Hispanic/Latino ethnicity (HR=0.70), preoperative opioid use (HR=0.58), elevated serum sodium (HR=0.97), and Tdap vaccination (HR=0.82). Postoperative AKI was associated with increased 30-day risk of myocardial infarction (RR=8.01), sepsis (RR=5.99), respiratory failure (RR=5.30), arrhythmia (RR=2.22), deep vein thrombosis (RR=1.98), transfusion (RR=1.92), and mortality (RR=2.22). Conclusions Postoperative AKI was independently associated with increased short-term morbidity and mortality following extracapsular hip fracture surgery in older adults. Recognition of perioperative risk factors may support earlier identification and targeted strategies to

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted using the TriNetX analytics platform (Cambridge, Massachusetts), a federated electronic health record (EHR) network that aggregates de-identified patient data from 109 healthcare organizations (HCOs) across the U.S. This analysis accessed data from 52 HCOs on July 30, 2025. Because the data are de-identified, this study was exempt from Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval and was conducted in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Patients aged ≥ 65 years who underwent surgical treatment of extracapsular hip fractures, specifically intertrochanteric, peritrochanteric, and subtrochanteric femur fractures, between January 1, 2015 and July 30, 2025 were included. This timeframe was selected to ensure diagnostic consistency following the adoption of the International Classification of Disease, 10 th Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) in the U.S. Surgical patients were identified using

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: of the International Classification of Disease, 10 th Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) in the U.S. Surgical patients were identified using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes 27244 and 27245. Patients were excluded if they had a diagnosis of AKI (ICD-10-CM N17) at least one day prior to the date of surgery. Two cohorts were created: the AKI cohort included patients diagnosed with AKI within seven days following hip fracture surgery, and the non-AKI cohort included patients without an AKI diagnosis within this postoperative window. The index event was defined as the date of hip fracture surgery to ensure the AKI was related to the fracture. Data extracted included demographics, comorbid diagnoses, laboratory values, vital signs, medications, and procedures, and diagnoses identified using ICD-10-CM codes. Laboratory values and vital signs were grouped using TriNetX-curated codes, medications were classified using the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC), Veterans

text: and vital signs were grouped using TriNetX-curated codes, medications were classified using the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC), Veterans Affairs (VA), and RxNorm coding systems, and procedures were identified using CPT codes ( Supplemental Material 1 ). To reduce confounding, 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching (PSM) without replacement was performed using the Compare Outcomes tool. Matching variables included components of the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) ( Supplemental Material 2 ). All covariates were time-restricted to data collected up to one day before surgery. Balance between matched cohorts was evaluated using density plots and standardized mean differences (SMDs). Preoperative characteristics were compared before and after matching using the Baseline Comparison tool. Variables were selected, time-restricted, and binned according to clinically relevant cutoffs. Results were reported as means ± standard deviations (SD), counts, percentages, p values, and

text: and binned according to clinically relevant cutoffs. Results were reported as means ± standard deviations (SD), counts, percentages, p values, and SMDs. A Cox proportional hazards model was used to identify independent predictors of postoperative AKI. Covariates were categorized as binary or continuous and were selected and time-restricted in the same manner as the baseline comparison ( Supplemental Material 1 ). The outcome was postoperative AKI (ICD-10-CM N17) occurring from the date of surgery to 30 days postoperatively. Model outputs included hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), standard errors (SE), and p values. Postoperative complications occurring within 0-30 days of surgery were assessed using the Explore Outcomes tool. Events were selected for clinical relevance ( Supplemental Material 3 ) and analyzed individually using two statistical methods: Measures of Association, which reported risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and odds ratios (OR) with 95%

Patients with pre-existing outcomes were excluded from analyses.

text: Discussion This large, multi-center cohort study of adults aged ≥ 65 years undergoing surgical treatment of extracapsular hip fractures found postoperative AKI to be a common complication associated with significantly increased risks of short-term adverse outcomes. Matched analyses identified nonmodifiable predictors of postoperative AKI to be Black or African American and White race and modifiable predictors to be elevated preoperative chloride, bicarbonate, SCr, and decreased preoperative serum protein levels. Conversely, Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, preoperative Tdap vaccination, preoperative opioid use, and elevated preoperative serum sodium levels were protective, though these associations warrant further investigation. Patients who developed postoperative AKI experienced significantly higher 30-day risks of MI, sepsis, respiratory failure, stroke, arrhythmia, DVT, blood transfusion, and mortality. Prior studies have identified an association between preoperative electrolyte

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: failure, stroke, arrhythmia, DVT, blood transfusion, and mortality. Prior studies have identified an association between preoperative electrolyte abnormalities and postoperative AKI within the orthopaedic population. 9 , 19 Additionally, a relationship between impaired baseline renal function, including increased preoperative SCr and bicarbonate levels, has been established by prior research in both general surgical and orthopaedic populations. 5 , 7 , 11 , 13 , 19 The present study supports these findings, highlighting the importance of electrolyte balance and renal stabilization prior to hip fracture surgery in this high-risk population. Notably, this study found increased preoperative serum sodium to be a protective factor against postoperative AKI. This finding warrants future investigation given the identification of electrolyte abnormalities and baseline renal function as risk factors for postoperative AKI. The association between preoperative anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and

text: abnormalities and baseline renal function as risk factors for postoperative AKI. The association between preoperative anemia, hypoalbuminemia, and hypoproteinemia has been established previously. 6 , 7 , 20 This study found reduced preoperative serum protein levels to be an independent risk factor for postoperative AKI, reflecting the importance of hemodynamic stabilization. Prior studies have found hip fracture patients who developed postoperative AKI to have higher morbidity rates and comorbidity burden, specifically cardiovascular complications, thromboembolism, and respiratory failure. 12 The present study also found postoperative AKI patients had higher rates of similar complications. These findings reflect the necessity of adequate screening protocols for AKI in this high-risk population, as well as the need for preventative measures prior to hip fracture surgery. Of note, the current study identified Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, preoperative opioid use, and Tdap vaccination as

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: prior to hip fracture surgery. Of note, the current study identified Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, preoperative opioid use, and Tdap vaccination as predictors of postoperative AKI. These findings should be interpreted with caution and are best considered hypothesis-generating. Current literature does not strongly support these associations, and they may reflect unmeasured confounders or proxies for other factors such as healthcare access, baseline medical optimization, or differences in perioperative monitoring. Further investigation is necessary to determine whether these associations represent true protective effects or residual confounding. These findings have important clinical implications for perioperative risk stratification in older adults undergoing hip fracture surgery. Several of the identified predictors of AKI, including electrolyte abnormalities and decreased serum protein levels, represent potentially modifiable preoperative factors. Optimization of fluid status,

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: electrolyte abnormalities and decreased serum protein levels, represent potentially modifiable preoperative factors. Optimization of fluid status, correction of electrolyte imbalances, and attention to nutritional status prior to surgery may help reduce the risk of postoperative AKI in this high-risk population. Because many of these laboratory markers are routinely obtained during preoperative evaluation, they may serve as practical indicators to guide perioperative optimization strategies to help mitigate the risk of postoperative AKI. This study had several limitations. First, the use of ICD-10-CM codes to define AKI may under detect subclinical AKI and does not differentiate between AKI stages or severity. Second, the retrospective design precludes causal inference, and residual confounding may persist despite PSM. Third, key intraoperative variables could not be accessed by the TriNetX platform. Finally, coding variations and site-level differences may cause residual bias.

Despite these weaknesses, this study identified several predictors and outcomes of postoperative AKI that strengthen prior studies, as well as various possibly novel variables that warrant further investigation.

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: Conclusions Postoperative AKI was independently associated with increased short-term morbidity and mortality following extracapsular hip fracture surgery in older adults. Recognition of perioperative risk factors may support earlier identification and targeted strategies to reduce AKI incidence and improve postoperative outcomes.

title: Predictors of Acute Kidney Injury in Older Adults With Extracapsular Hip Fractures
text: Conclusion Postoperative AKI is a frequent and clinically significant complication among older adults undergoing extracapsular hip fracture surgery. This study identified several independent predictors, including preoperative serum markers, race, and comorbid conditions, and highlighted a substantially increased risk of short-term complications and mortality in patients who developed AKI. A future meta-analysis that affirms all predictors induced in this study as well as previous studies that these findings highlight would also be particularly useful. These findings underscore the need for improved preoperative risk stratification and tailored interventions aimed at reducing the incidence and downstream consequences of postoperative AKI in this high-risk population.

text: ABSTRACT Objective The clinical efficacy and early outcomes of total arch replacement with frozen elephant trunk (TAR+FET) in elderly patients presenting with acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) remain incompletely characterized. This study aimed to comprehensively evaluate early clinical outcomes and perioperative risk profiles in elderly patients undergoing TAR+FET for ATAAD, thereby addressing gaps in the literature and providing evidence to guide surgical decision‐making in this high‐risk population. Methods A multicenter retrospective analysis was conducted involving 1634 patients who underwent TAR+FET for ATAAD between 2015 and 2023 across seven cardiovascular centers. Patients were categorized into elderly (≥ 60 years, n = 258) and non‐elderly (< 60 years, n = 1376) groups. Baseline characteristics, operative details, and early outcomes were compared between groups before propensity score matching (PSM). A 1:2 PSM established a balanced cohort of 699 patients (elderly, n

A 1:2 PSM established a balanced cohort of 699 patients (elderly, n = 245; non‐elderly, n = 454), in which postoperative complications and survival were compared. To evaluate the independent prognostic impact of age, multivariable Cox proportional hazards models with incremental covariate adjustments were applied. Results Before PSM, elderly patients had higher prevalences of coronary artery disease, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, with significantly longer intensive care unit (ICU) stay, prolonged ventilation time, and lower 30‐day survival compared with non‐elderly patients. After PSM, baseline covariates were well balanced; however, elderly patients continued to demonstrate worse perioperative outcomes, including longer ICU stay (68 [35–162] vs. 47 [28–113] h, p = 0.001), prolonged ventilation time (49 [21–111] vs. 38 [18–86] h, p < 0.001), and higher incidences of reintubation, tracheostomy, respiratory

text: h, p = 0.001), prolonged ventilation time (49 [21–111] vs. 38 [18–86] h, p < 0.001), and higher incidences of reintubation, tracheostomy, respiratory failure, acute kidney injury (AKI), and dialysis (all p < 0.010). Kaplan–Meier analysis revealed significantly lower 30‐day survival in the elderly group (86.5% vs. 93.6%, p = 0.002). Multivariable Cox regression identified age ≥ 60 years as an independent predictor of mortality (hazard ratio = 2.286, 95% confidence interval: 1.361–3.840, p = 0.002). Within the elderly subgroup, non‐survivors were older, had longer operative and cardiopulmonary bypass times, and experienced substantially higher rates of severe postoperative complications—particularly neurological injury, dialysis‐requiring AKI, arrhythmia, and respiratory failure—than survivors. Conclusion Even after adjustment for baseline characteristics, elderly patients undergoing TAR+FET have higher risks of perioperative complications and early mortality than non‐elderly patients.

At all participating centers, TAR+FET, following Sun's procedure, was used as the standard operative strategy, with broadly consistent intraoperative cerebral protection principles. Between January 2015 and December 2023, 1911 consecutive patients diagnosed with type A aortic dissection and treated with TAR+FET were screened. Patients with (1) subacute or chronic type A dissection, or (2) incomplete essential clinical or imaging data were excluded. Therefore, all primary analyses were performed using a complete‐case dataset. After applying these criteria, 1634 patients with ATAAD were eligible for analysis. Patients were stratified by age into two groups: elderly (≥ 60 years, n = 258) and non‐elderly (< 60 years, n = 1376). Subacute (15–90 days) and chronic (> 90 days) dissections were excluded. The primary endpoint was all‐cause 30‐day mortality. Thirty‐day mortality status was available for all patients in the analytic cohort. Secondary endpoints included major postoperative complications: reintubation, tracheostomy, stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic), dialysis‐requiring acute kidney injury (AKI), respiratory failure, low cardiac output syndrome, arrhythmia, limb ischemia, cardiac tamponade, and reoperation for postoperative bleeding. All postoperative complications were assessed during the index hospitalization, defined as the period from the date of operation to hospital discharge or in‐hospital death. AKI was defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria as an increase in serum creatinine by ≥ 0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, an increase to ≥ 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥ 6 h. Dialysis‐dependent AKI was defined as initiation of renal replacement therapy post‐surgery during index hospitalization. Neurological complications were classified as stroke, defined as a new permanent neurological deficit confirmed by imaging (ischemic or hemorrhagic), or temporary neurological dysfunction, defined as reversible neurological symptoms without radiographic evidence of cerebral injury. Selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP) was applied during hypothermic circulatory arrest, with nasopharyngeal temperature individualized within a moderate‐to‐low hypothermia range according to patient condition and perfusion strategy. text: 4 Discussion In this large multicenter cohort spanning seven cardiovascular centers and managed under a standardized TAR+FET protocol, elderly patients (≥ 60 years) had significantly higher 30‐day mortality than non‐elderly patients after PSM (13.5% vs. 6.4%). In fully adjusted Cox models, age ≥ 60 years remained an independent predictor of 30‐day mortality (HR = 2.286, 95% CI: 1.361–3.840; p = 0.002). The divergence in survival rates became evident within the first postoperative week and persisted through 30 days. Among elderly patients, non‐survivors had longer operative and CPB times, required more prolonged ventilation, and had a higher incidence of tracheostomy. They also experienced significantly higher rates of major complications, including stroke, limb ischemia, dialysis‐dependent AKI, and respiratory failure. Collectively, these findings suggest that increased perioperative vulnerability, rather than procedural factors alone, contribute to the elevated early mortality

In our cohort, the median age at diagnosis was relatively young (49 years), consistent with contemporary Chinese registries reporting similar age distributions (Sino‐RAD, 49 ± 11.1 years; a national multicenter registry, 51.6 ± 11.7 years). In contrast, major Western datasets report substantially higher ages at presentation, typically in the early 60s (IRAD, 61.5 ± 14.6 years; NORCAAD, 61.5 ± 12.1 years; GERAADA, 61.4 ± 13.5 years). This geographic disparity should be considered when extrapolating findings and establishing age‐stratified benchmarks [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ]. Beyond demographic differences, biological mechanisms of aging may also contribute to the development and prognosis of aortic dissection. Recent studies indicate that degenerative programs mediated by activator protein‐1 in vascular

Recent studies indicate that degenerative programs mediated by activator protein‐1 in vascular smooth muscle cells, the age‐related miR‐1204—MYLK axis, and broader pathways involving senescence and extracellular matrix remodeling increase vulnerability of the aortic wall, thereby linking aging to both disease susceptibility and prognosis [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ]. Building on this demographic and biological framework, we evaluated the impact of age on surgical outcomes. In experienced centers, short‐term outcomes following TAR+FET are generally acceptable. A representative large TAR+FET series using the Sun's procedure reported early mortality of 7.8%, with major neurologic or spinal complications in the single digits [ 3 ]. A meta‐analysis of TAR+FET for ATAAD reported a pooled early mortality of 9.2%, with similarly low rates of major neurologic events [ 4 ]. Our multicenter cohort, managed with a uniform operative strategy, is

Our multicenter cohort, managed with a uniform operative strategy, is consistent with these benchmarks, with an overall 30‐day mortality of 7.1%. Importantly, our study extends prior work in three ways. First, by combining 1:2 PSM with fully adjusted Cox models, we more precisely isolate the association of age with early mortality. Second, time‐resolved analyses show that survival differences emerge within the first postoperative week and persist through 30 days. Third, within the elderly subgroup, we characterize early failure by comparing survivors and non‐survivors, identifying longer operative and CPB times, greater ventilatory support with higher tracheostomy rates, and significantly increased rates of stroke, limb ischemia, dialysis‐dependent AKI, and respiratory failure. Physiologic reserve refers to the capacity of multiple organ systems to tolerate and recover from major stress, whereas frailty represents a clinically meaningful state of vulnerability resulting from diminished reserve across systems [ 20 ]. Clinically, frailty can be screened using bedside tools such as the Clinical Frailty Scale [ 21 ]. Evidence from surgical cohorts indicates that preoperative frailty predicts postoperative complications and resource utilization, underscoring its relevance to perioperative risk stratification in older patients [ 22 ]. In cardiac surgery, frailty assessment provides prognostic information beyond conventional risk models and supports more informed perioperative counseling and shared decision‐making [ 23 ]. Among the elderly, non‐survivors had a higher prevalence of preexisting cerebrovascular disease, underwent longer surgical and CPB durations (8.0 vs. 7.5 h; 211 vs. 193 min), required prolonged ventilation with more frequent tracheostomy, and experienced higher rates of stroke, limb ischemia, dialysis‐requiring AKI, respiratory failure, and ECMO use. These findings align with previous research showing that cerebrovascular disease and prolonged CPB or cerebral perfusion increase the risk of postoperative stroke after type A or arch repair [ 24 ]. Furthermore, dialysis‐requiring AKI is a strong predictor of early mortality [ 25 ], postoperative tracheostomy identifies a high‐risk subgroup [ 26 ], and ECMO use after ATAAD is associated with significantly elevated in‐hospital mortality and

text: tracheostomy identifies a high‐risk subgroup [ 26 ], and ECMO use after ATAAD is associated with significantly elevated in‐hospital mortality and complications [ 27 ]. Together with evidence from the frailty literature demonstrating greater perioperative vulnerability in older cardiac patients [ 28 ], our findings support multi‐organ vulnerability, rather than procedural complexity alone, as the principal driver of early mortality in the elderly. We hypothesize that elderly patients face increased early risk following TAR+FET due to three interrelated mechanisms. First, lower physiologic reserve associated with aging and frailty limits tolerance to surgical stress; simple bedside frailty measures provide prognostic information beyond conventional risk scores and help explain why some older patients deteriorate despite standardized care [ 29 ]. Second, exposure to CPB and hypothermia triggers a systemic stress response characterized by inflammation, endothelial injury, increased

text: care [ 29 ]. Second, exposure to CPB and hypothermia triggers a systemic stress response characterized by inflammation, endothelial injury, increased capillary permeability, and impaired microcirculatory flow, from which the brain, kidneys, and lungs of older adults recover less effectively [ 30 ]. Third, the impact of operative duration and procedural complexity is amplified in elderly patients. TAR+FET requires multiple anastomoses and cerebral‐protection maneuvers; contemporary series report CPB times of approximately 170–200 min and cross‐clamp times of 85–110 min, although “branch‐first” strategies may reduce these intervals [ 31 ]. Prolonged CPB, cerebral perfusion, or circulatory arrest is associated with increased stroke risk and organ injury after type A/arch repair [ 24 ], and longer CPB is linked to AKI and higher in‐hospital mortality, including in total‐arch cohorts where “extended CPB” is an independent risk factor [ 32 ]. Even modest delays may be clinically meaningful

Even modest delays may be clinically meaningful in frail older adults; both earlier and contemporary studies suggest that simplifying or accelerating arch strategies is advantageous in octogenarians [ 31 , 33 ]. Clinically, the excess risk associated with advanced age likely reflects diminished physiologic reserve combined with greater baseline cerebrovascular, renal, and pulmonary vulnerability, which reduces tolerance to CPB, hypothermia, and prolonged ventilation and predisposes patients to early multi‐organ dysfunction. Accordingly, perioperative management in older patients should prioritize vigilant neurologic monitoring, proactive organ‐protective strategies, and early escalation of supportive care when clinical deterioration is suspected. text: suspected. Based on the vulnerability–stress framework, perioperative care should follow a comprehensive protocol to attenuate the initial insult and prevent secondary complications. For arrhythmia management, continuous telemetry and strict electrolyte control are essential. Continuation or initiation of β‐blocker therapy is recommended, and QT‐prolonging medications should be avoided. Clinically significant arrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation and ventricular tachyarrhythmias, should be managed according to established guideline‐based algorithms, with temporary pacing or defibrillation for hemodynamic instability [ 34 ]. For cerebral protection, moderate hypothermia combined with antegrade cerebral perfusion should be employed, along with strict blood pressure control, meticulous de‐airing, gradual rewarming, and scheduled neurological assessments during the first postoperative week, with prompt imaging for any emergent deficits [ 2 ]. For renal protection, a KDIGO‐based prevention should be implemented, including goal‐directed mean arterial pressure, maintenance of euvolemia, avoidance of nephrotoxins, close monitoring of urine output and serum creatinine, and glycemic control. Early initiation of renal replacement therapy should be considered in cases of persistent oliguria or rising creatinine accompanied by fluid overload [ 35 ]. For pulmonary protection, lung‐protective ventilation (6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight) with adequate positive end‐expiratory pressure and low driving pressure is recommended, along with avoidance of positive fluid balance, early but safe extubation, early mobilization, and effective analgesia [ 36 ]. TAR+FET procedures inherently necessitate hypothermic circulatory arrest and prolonged CPB, both of which are associated with increased risks of neurologic events, AKI, pulmonary complications, and in‐hospital mortality. Prolonged circulatory arrest and CPB duration have been correlated with higher incidences of stroke and AKI in cohorts undergoing arch surgery [ 30 , 37 ]. Consequently, in elderly or frail patients, or when distal aortic involvement is limited, strategies that minimize exposure to CPB and hypothermic circulatory arrest are preferable. Such strategies include initial proximal repair followed by staged TEVAR and type II hybrid arch repair, both of which have demonstrated acceptable safety and efficacy in elderly or complex cases [ 38 , 39 ]. Experienced centers have also reported near‐normothermic/limited‐arrest FET techniques to further mitigate physiologic stress [ 40 ]. text: 5 Conclusion In this multicenter cohort of patients with ATAAD treated with TAR+FET, age ≥ 60 years independently predicted higher 30‐day mortality and complication burden, with divergence emerging during the first postoperative week. Given broadly comparable operative metrics across age groups, the excess early risk likely reflects reduced physiologic reserve. Accordingly, careful procedure selection and rigorous organ‐protective perioperative strategies should be emphasized in elderly patients.

title: Long-term LDL cholesterol burden and stroke: mechanistic insights and emerging strategies for personalized lipid management
text: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a causal and modifiable driver of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and an important contributor to atherosclerotic ischemic stroke. Increasing evidence suggests that cumulative LDL-C exposure—the combined effect of LDL-C magnitude and duration over time—captures vascular injury more accurately than a single measurement obtained at one clinical encounter. This review uses cumulative LDL-C exposure as an organizing framework for stroke prevention. We summarize current approaches to quantifying long-term LDL-C burden, review epidemiological evidence linking cumulative exposure to incident and recurrent ischemic stroke, and discuss biological mechanisms that may explain these associations. We then examine how lipid-lowering therapies, including statins, PCSK9 inhibitors, and small-interfering RNA-based agents, may reduce cumulative vascular injury. Particular attention is paid to the clinical challenge of balancing ischemic benefit

title: Long-term LDL cholesterol burden and stroke: mechanistic insights and emerging strategies for personalized lipid management
text: RNA-based agents, may reduce cumulative vascular injury. Particular attention is paid to the clinical challenge of balancing ischemic benefit against potential hemorrhagic vulnerability in selected high-risk phenotypes, such as patients with probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy or multiple lobar cerebral microbleeds. We propose a precision-management framework that integrates longitudinal lipid exposure, stroke subtype, genetics, neuroimaging, and dynamic risk assessment. By shifting attention from static lipid values to lifelong exposure, cumulative LDL-C burden may offer a more coherent basis for individualized cerebrovascular prevention.

text: 2 Quantifying cumulative LDL-C exposure: methods and challenges A meaningful discussion of cumulative LDL-C burden begins with measurement. LDL-C changes over time in response to aging, diet, treatment intensity, adherence, and genetic background. Accordingly, different analytic approaches have been developed to estimate long- term exposure. 2.1 Classical estimation models The simplest historical approach treats cumulative exposure as a rough product of age and LDL-C level. Although intuitive, this approximation ignores time-varying treatment effects and does not reflect the true shape of LDL-C trajectories. More informative approaches use repeated measurements to estimate a time-weighted average (TWA), cumulative burden above a predefined threshold, or area-under-the-curve-like metrics derived from serial LDL-C values. These methods better capture the longitudinal nature of exposure and have been used in major cohort analyses evaluating cardiovascular and cerebrovascular outcomes ( 5

text: capture the longitudinal nature of exposure and have been used in major cohort analyses evaluating cardiovascular and cerebrovascular outcomes ( 5 , 6 ). 2.2 Emerging techniques and remaining limitations More recent approaches extend beyond repeated averages and attempt to reconstruct life-course exposure more explicitly. These include trajectory-based models, threshold-based burden models, and genetics-informed estimates that infer lifelong LDL-C exposure from inherited variation. Such approaches are conceptually appealing because they align more closely with the biological hypothesis that arterial injury accumulates gradually over time. However, they also have important limitations. Most require dense longitudinal data, assumptions about missing values and treatment adherence, and careful handling of regression dilution bias and survivor bias. In addition, no universal threshold defines “high cumulative LDL-C burden,” and different studies operationalize this concept differently.

title: Long-term LDL cholesterol burden and stroke: mechanistic insights and emerging strategies for personalized lipid management
text: bias. In addition, no universal threshold defines “high cumulative LDL-C burden,” and different studies operationalize this concept differently. For stroke research, this lack of standardization matters. The apparent strength of the association between cumulative LDL-C burden and stroke risk will depend partly on how well long-term exposure is measured. Future studies should therefore move toward integrated models that combine serial LDL-C values with treatment history, adherence, polygenic susceptibility, and imaging markers of vascular injury. At present, a repeated-measure time-weighted average or area-under-the-curve-like metric may be the most practical choice for stroke-oriented research because it can be derived from routinely collected serial LDL-C values while still capturing both intensity and duration of exposure ( 5 , 6 ). Until such methods are standardized, cumulative exposure should be viewed as a promising but still methodologically evolving construct.

title: Long-term LDL cholesterol burden and stroke: mechanistic insights and emerging strategies for personalized lipid management
text: 7 Conclusion Cumulative LDL-C exposure offers a more biologically and clinically informative framework for cerebrovascular risk assessment than single time-point lipid measurement. Available evidence supports its association with ischemic stroke, particularly atherosclerotic stroke, and with recurrent vascular events after stroke. This relationship is mechanistically plausible through chronic effects on plaque vulnerability, endothelial and blood–brain barrier integrity, inflammation, and thrombosis. Clinically, the concept reinforces the importance of early and sustained LDL-C lowering while also highlighting the need for individualized treatment intensity in patients with competing hemorrhagic vulnerability. Future progress will depend on better measurement of cumulative exposure and on integrating lipid burden with genetics, imaging, and dynamic risk prediction.

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: Background Acute myocardial infarction (MI) is associated with subsequent cognitive decline. Whether detection of prior MI using routine electrocardiogram (ECG) and self-reported history can identify different trajectories of cognitive decline is uncertain. We sought to determine the association between prior MI and longitudinal cognitive assessments within a national, biracial cohort study. Methods We included participants in the Reasons for Geographic and Racial Differences in Stroke (REGARDS) cohort, enrolled from 2003–2007, who had an interpretable ECG and no baseline cognitive impairment. Prior MI at baseline was determined by self-reported history and ECG evidence of MI. Individuals were subdivided into self-reported (no Q-wave with MI history), clinical (Q-wave with MI history), and silent MI (Q-wave without MI history). We examined the interaction between prior MI and longitudinal change in global cognitive function, assessed by annual telephone-based Six-Item Screener scores,

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: the interaction between prior MI and longitudinal change in global cognitive function, assessed by annual telephone-based Six-Item Screener scores, using linear mixed-effects models adjusted for demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and incident cardiovascular events with censoring for death. Results The primary analytic cohort consisted of 20923 individuals followed over a median of 10.1 years with 2183 having evidence of prior MI at baseline (1098 self-reported, 281 clinical, and 804 silent MI). A total of 4884 of participants died during follow-up and were censored at the time of death. Prior MI was associated with an excess adjusted annual decline of global cognition (−0.016 points; 95% CI −0.021, −0.012; interaction p<0.001). Similar trajectories of accelerated annual global cognitive decline were seen with self-reported (−0.016 points; 95% CI −0.022, −0.010; interaction p<0.001), clinical (−0.020 points; 95% CI −0.032, −0.008; interaction p=0.001), and silent (−0.015

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: (−0.016 points; 95% CI −0.022, −0.010; interaction p<0.001), clinical (−0.020 points; 95% CI −0.032, −0.008; interaction p=0.001), and silent (−0.015 points; 95% CI −0.022, −0.008; interaction p<0.001) MI. Conclusion Evidence of prior MI, whether clinically recognized or silent, was associated with an accelerated decline in global cognition. Prior MI may identify individuals at risk for future cognitive impairment.

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: Methods Data Availability Requests for primary data should be sent to the REGARDS study at regardsadmin@uab.edu . Details of the study data access policy may be found at www.regardsstudy.org . Alexander Merkler accepts responsibility for accuracy of the results. Population The REGARDS study is an ongoing biracial, longitudinal cohort study aimed to investigate the elevated stroke mortality within the stroke belt of the southeastern US (North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, and Louisiana) and among Black Americans. 10 The study enrolled 30239 Black or White Americans 45 years of age and older from January 2003 to October 2007, with oversampling from the stroke belt region and Black individuals. Recruitment was performed via random selection from a commercially available nationwide list via mail and telephone. Exclusion criteria for REGARDS included active cancer therapy, any medical conditions precluding long-term follow-up, active or

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: mail and telephone. Exclusion criteria for REGARDS included active cancer therapy, any medical conditions precluding long-term follow-up, active or pending residence within a nursing home, or inability to speak English. A computer-assisted telephone interview was performed at intake to collect medical history. Participants underwent a subsequent in-home examination including height, weight, blood pressure, ECG, medication inventory, fasting blood sample, and urine collection. Participants are followed every 6 months with structured telephone interviews. For this analysis, only REGARDS participants with available baseline interview data, MI status, Six-Item Screener (SIS) at baseline and follow-up, and interpretable ECG data were included. Individuals with baseline global cognitive impairment (SIS score< 5) or those who experienced an incident cardiovascular event (stroke, heart failure exacerbation, MI, coronary revascularization procedure) between enrollment and initial SIS
