text: an incident cardiovascular event (stroke, heart failure exacerbation, MI, coronary revascularization procedure) between enrollment and initial SIS assessment were excluded. All participants provided written informed consent. Study approval was granted by the institutional review boards of all participating, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Results were reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline. 11 Exposure: Prior Myocardial Infarction Assessment At the time of the initial intake interview, participants were asked whether they had been previously diagnosed with MI by a physician. During the subsequent in-home examination, a 7-lead ECG was performed until April 2004, after which a 12-lead ECG was used. Electrocardiographs captured at a standard 25 mm/s speed and were calibrated to 10mm=1 mV. Recordings were transferred for central reading by research staff blinded to cognitive data

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: standard 25 mm/s speed and were calibrated to 10mm=1 mV. Recordings were transferred for central reading by research staff blinded to cognitive data (Epidemiological Cardiology Research Center, Wake Forest School of Medicine, Winston-Salem, NC, USA). Evidence of MI was standardized by the Minnesota code (MC) scheme as major Q/QS wave abnormalities (MC 1–1-X through 1–2-X) or smaller Q/QS wave abnormalities (MC 1–3-X) with major ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities (MC 4–1,4–2,5–1, or 5–2). 12 Interpretation was performed by a certified coder, senior coder, and center PI. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or through a separate senior coder if uncertainty remained. 10 Participants with a baseline QRS duration ≥120 msec were excluded from the analysis due to inability of ECG Minnesota code to accurately reflect prior Q-wave MI in the presence of left bundle branch block or ventricular-paced rhythms. Silent MI was defined as the presence of ECG evidence of MI in the absence of

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: the presence of left bundle branch block or ventricular-paced rhythms. Silent MI was defined as the presence of ECG evidence of MI in the absence of a self-reported diagnosis. Self-reported MI was defined as a self-reported physician diagnosis of MI and no ECG evidence of MI. Clinical MI was defined as the combination of both ECG evidence and a self-reported history of MI. Participants without a self-reported history and no ECG evidence of MI were classified as no MI. Both binary and categorical exposure variables were created to classify prior MI status. The binary variable dichotomized participants as having a prior MI (silent, self-reported, or clinical) or no MI. The categorical variable labeled participants as either silent, self-reported, clinical, or no MI. Cognitive assessments The REGARDS study incorporated telephone-based cognitive assessments by trained research staff. 13 For all participants enrolled after December 2003, a global cognitive screen using the Six-Item

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: cognitive assessments by trained research staff. 13 For all participants enrolled after December 2003, a global cognitive screen using the Six-Item Screener (SIS) was conducted at enrollment and annually thereafter. All assessments conducted until December 31, 2017 were included in this analysis. The SIS is a validated screening tool with an immediate three-item recall and three temporal orientation items. Scores range from 0 to 6 with a score of less than 5 indicating cognitive impairment (mild cognitive impairment or dementia). Compared to a complete cognitive assessment battery performed by a physician, the sensitivity and specificity to detect cognitive impairment at a threshold of less than 5 points within community-dwelling individuals is 74% and 80%, respectively. Using the SIS to assess dementia alone, a threshold of less than 4 points demonstrates a sensitivity and specificity of 89% and 88%, respectively. 14 A three-test battery was introduced in 2006 and administered in

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: 4 points demonstrates a sensitivity and specificity of 89% and 88%, respectively. 14 A three-test battery was introduced in 2006 and administered in two-year intervals. The battery includes the animal fluency test (AFT), the word list learning (WLL), and the word list delayed recall (WLD) from the consortium to establish a registry for Alzheimer’s disease (CERAD) battery. 15 The AFT is a measure of executive function and is scored as the number of animals named within 60 seconds. The WLL and WLD are measures of learning and memory, respectively. The WLL score ranges from 0–30 and is the sum of immediate recall across three trials of a 10-item word list. After the last learning trial, non-cognitive interview questions are performed for 5 minutes and then the participant is asked to recall the word list, resulting in a WLD score ranging from 0–10. These cognitive measures are in accordance with those established by the Vascular Cognitive Impairment Harmonization Standards. 16 For all

text: from 0–10. These cognitive measures are in accordance with those established by the Vascular Cognitive Impairment Harmonization Standards. 16 For all assessments, test scores were modeled as continuous outcomes, with lower scores indicating worse cognitive performance. Sex, race (Black or White), region (stroke belt, stroke buckle, or non-stroke belt), highest-achieved level of education (less than high school, high school graduate, some college, college graduate and above), and annual income (less than $20000, $20000-$34999, $35000-$74999, greater than $75000, or non-disclosed) were self-reported. All follow-up assessments for incident stroke, heart failure, MI, or coronary revascularization until December 31, 2017 were included in this analysis. Absolute standardized differences were calculated to describe differences in characteristics between groups. The relationship between prior MI (binary exposure) with longitudinal changes in SIS scores was examined with a linear mixed-effects model including an interaction variable of baseline MI status and time (years from date of first cognitive measurement). Participants were censored at the time of death or last follow up. Crude models accounted for only baseline MI status, time, and interaction of MI status and time. Adjusted models were additionally fit using age, sex, race, geographic region, education, income, exercise frequency, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, systolic blood

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: were additionally fit using age, sex, race, geographic region, education, income, exercise frequency, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, systolic blood pressure, eGFR, alcohol use, current smoking, CES-D-4, atrial fibrillation, previous coronary revascularization, and incident cardiovascular events. The primary analysis included only subjects with complete covariate data. Subject-specific random effect terms accounted for correlation of cognitive measures within participants over time and allowed for participant-specific rates of cognitive change in all models. In these models, the interaction between MI status and time can be interpreted as the excess annual rate of cognitive decline associated with MI. Models were repeated with categorical exposure reflecting MI subtypes. From the adjusted model, we calculated participant-specific predicted values for each cognitive assessment over time for a theoretical representative participant. Selecting mean values for continuous variables and mode for categorical variables, we plotted trajectories of a theoretical participant. Random effects for this prediction were set to zero. Three secondary analyses were conducted to assess: 1) the association between MI and incident cognitive impairment (SIS score< 5) using mixed-effect logistic regression; 2) the association between MI and incident severe cognitive impairment (SIS score< 4) using mixed-effect logistic regression; 3) the association of prior MI status on longitudinal changes in each specific cognitive domain assessments (AFT, WLL, and WLD); 4) differences between sex and race through a stratified subgroup analysis. Statistical significance for all analyses was set at two-sided p-value <0.05. All analyses were performed using STATA version 15 (StataCorp, Cary, NC).

text: Results Baseline Characteristics Of the 30239 participants of the REGARDS cohort, 6896 participants did not meet inclusion criteria and 2420 were missing covariate data. The analytic cohort consisted of 20923 participants with a median age of 63 (IQR 57–70) years and composed of 12937 (61.8%) White, 7986 (38.2%) Black, 11960 (57.2%) female, and 8963 (42.8%) male individuals. Evidence of any MI was present in 2183 (10.4%) of participants with 1098 self-reported (5.2%), 281 clinical (1.3%), and 804 silent MI (3.8%). A greater proportion of individuals with evidence of prior MI had cardiovascular risk factors. Over the follow-up period, a total of 4884 of participants died (23.3%) with a higher mortality observed among participants with prior MI (44.4% vs 20.9%). title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: Discussion In this study, evidence of a prior MI was associated with an excess rate of cognitive decline and incident cognitive impairment. This is the first study to investigate the impact of both recognized (clinical or self-reported) and silent MI on cognitive decline in a large, biracial, population within the United States. As an accelerated rate of cognitive decline is a herald for future dementia, this study suggests potential for routine ECG and self-reported history to identify a subgroup of the population at elevated risk for loss of cognitive function. 24 This study adds to existing literature supporting the association between coronary heart disease and cognitive impairment. Previous investigations of incident coronary ischemic events have demonstrated that the impact on cognitive function is not immediate but manifests as a subsequent accelerated rate of long-term cognitive decline. 3 , 25 , 26 Two separate meta-analysis of prospective studies demonstrated a 26% increase

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: subsequent accelerated rate of long-term cognitive decline. 3 , 25 , 26 Two separate meta-analysis of prospective studies demonstrated a 26% increase in risk of future dementia alone and a 45% increase risk of composite dementia, cognitive impairment, or cognitive decline among individuals with a diagnosis of coronary heart disease. 27 , 28 Within the REGARDS cohort, participants with evidence of a prior MI had a 5% annual increase in the relative odds of incident cognitive impairment. The development of interventions to decrease the burden of dementia requires identification of high risk, pre-symptomatic individuals using pragmatic assessments that may be implemented in both high and low resource settings. The definition of coronary heart disease varies across studies but typically relies upon self-reported history combined with supporting ECG, medical records, coronary revascularization, or laboratory testing. The simple scheme chosen in this analysis represents a clinically

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: supporting ECG, medical records, coronary revascularization, or laboratory testing. The simple scheme chosen in this analysis represents a clinically feasible approach to easily identify high-risk individuals applicable in a real-world setting. This is particularly relevant to fragmented health care systems where clinicians may not have access to medical records from prior events. The mechanism by which MI leads to cognitive impairment remains unclear. Individuals with prior MI have greater prevalence of vascular risk factors and are at an increased risk for subsequent cardiovascular events which are established risk factors for cognitive impairment. 29 , 30 We demonstrated a persistent accelerated rate of cognitive decline after adjustment for these factors and censoring incident cardiovascular events. Thus, comorbid cardiovascular disease alone did not completely explain the relation between MI and excessive deterioration of cognition. Plausible explanations include microvascular

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: alone did not completely explain the relation between MI and excessive deterioration of cognition. Plausible explanations include microvascular disease, silent cerebral infarcts, systemic inflammation, cerebral hypoperfusion, Glymphatic dysfunction, and impaired amyloid clearance. 31 , 32 Uncertainty remains regarding the pathology underlying cognitive decline after MI, and an increased risk for both Alzheimer’s and vascular dementia has been proposed. 33 , 34 The relative degree of impact within specific cognitive domains may provide some insight into the predominant underlying pathology in this population. 35 , 35 We observed a decline in executive function, learning, and memory among individuals with self-reported MI, yet a larger, isolated decline in memory was seen in those with clinical MI. The former pattern is consistent with vascular dementia whereas the latter is more typical of Alzheimer’s disease. Although these results were based upon a relatively small sample, this may

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: dementia whereas the latter is more typical of Alzheimer’s disease. Although these results were based upon a relatively small sample, this may represent heterogeneous underlying neurodegenerative pathologies in individuals with atherosclerotic disease 36 , 37 . The significant association between silent MI and excess cognitive decline is notable. Inconsistencies in the association of MI and cognitive decline among previous population-based studies may be attributed to the failure to include individuals with silent MI. In the REGARDS cohort, 36.8% of all participants with evidence of MI at study entry were clinically silent. Future investigations of coronary heart disease’s role in cognitive impairment should account for silent MI. Whether clinically recognized and silent MI impact cognition via alternative mechanisms remains unanswered. It has also been postulated that silent MI may represent a cardiac manifestation of broader systemic microvascular disease. Individuals with silent MI

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: has also been postulated that silent MI may represent a cardiac manifestation of broader systemic microvascular disease. Individuals with silent MI have a greater burden of small vessel disease in other vascular beds and reduced large vessel atherosclerotic burden compared to recognized MI. 38 , 39 The risk of ischemic stroke is greater in individuals with silent MI compared to those without evidence of MI, and an accrual of subclinical cerebral infarcts may be another contributory factor to cognitive deterioration. 40 , 41 The association between prior MI and accelerated cognitive decline was consistent across both race and sex. In contrast to the Rotterdam cohort, we demonstrated that silent MI was also associated with excess cognitive decline in females, similar to males. 9 The divergence in results may be attributed to our larger sample size, distinctive population characteristics, and alternative outcome measures. The Rotterdam investigators utilized incident dementia rather than

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: size, distinctive population characteristics, and alternative outcome measures. The Rotterdam investigators utilized incident dementia rather than serial cognitive assessment to detect longitudinal decline, which may be insensitive to detect more subtle cognitive deterioration. Clinical MI demonstrated a non-significant trend in females, likely due to the lower baseline prevalence of recognized MI among females. As observed in other populations, silent MI is more common among females and may be attributed to differences in nociceptive threshold tolerance or clinician misdiagnosis. 42 , 43 Future studies of silent cardiovascular events in females may identify important opportunities for prevention of cognitive decline. Limitations Several limitations of this study should be noted. Despite extensive adjustment for comorbid risk factors, demographics, and incident cardiovascular events, a possible effect of residual or unmeasured confounders remains. For example, although baseline age

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: demographics, and incident cardiovascular events, a possible effect of residual or unmeasured confounders remains. For example, although baseline age was adjusted for in all models, chronological age is likely an incomplete measure of the ageing process and may not reflect biologic age. 44 , 45 Thus the effect of older age in patients with prior MI may be underestimated in our models. Moreover, patients with MI had a greater observed mortality over the follow-up period, and earlier censoring due to death may have underestimated the effect of prior MI on cognitive decline. Generalizability of our findings is limited due to a lack of consistent ECG criteria of MI. 46 Although all ECGs within the REGARDS study were reviewed systematically by a team of independent coders using the Minnesota classification system, MI criteria are not uniform across other population studies. The REGARDS study defined Q-wave MI as both major and minor Q waves plus major ST/T wave abnormalities whereas other

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: across other population studies. The REGARDS study defined Q-wave MI as both major and minor Q waves plus major ST/T wave abnormalities whereas other cohorts include only major Q waves. Furthermore, ECG is known to have a relatively poor sensitivity in detection of prior MI, and it is possible that a significant proportion of silent MI were undetected with ECG. 47 Cardiac MRI is more sensitive in the detection of prior MI and may improve detection of silent MI. 48 While this study intentionally investigated a pragmatic definition of prior MI, the use of self-reported history introduces a risk of recall bias. Accuracy of self-reported history varies depending on the condition of interest; MI has been shown to have overall moderate sensitivity in agreement with medical records. 49 , 50 Lastly, the SIS is an abbreviated screening tool and is not a comprehensive cognitive assessment. Subtle declines in specific domains of cognition may not be captured by SIS, and it is unable to diagnose

title: Prior Myocardial Infarction and Cognitive Decline: The REGARDS Cohort
text: not a comprehensive cognitive assessment. Subtle declines in specific domains of cognition may not be captured by SIS, and it is unable to diagnose specific subtypes of dementia. Due to the limited numbers of domain-specific assessments and lower frequency of measurement, the results of domain specific analyses should be considered exploratory. Conclusion We found that evidence of a prior MI was associated with an accelerated rate of cognitive decline in a large national, biracial population. Using ECG and self-reported history may provide a pragmatic, low-cost strategy to identify individuals at elevated risk for cognitive decline.

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: Abstract INTRODUCTION Identifying precursors to mild cognitive impairment (MCI)—the transitional stage between unimpaired cognition and dementia—is a public health priority. While sensory and motor impairments are each linked to MCI, their integrated contribution as a sensorimotor construct remains underexplored. METHODS We analyzed cross‐sectional data from two US cohorts: Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC; n = 880) and Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA; n = 681), excluding individuals with stroke, Parkinson's disease, or dementia. A composite sensorimotor score—based on hearing, vision, olfaction, balance, gait speed, and grip strength—was created using factor analysis. Structural equation modeling assessed associations with MCI, adjusting for key covariates. RESULTS Higher sensorimotor function was associated with lower odds of MCI: ARIC odds ratio (OR) = 0.53 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.40–0.71); BLSA OR = 0.59 (95% CI: 0.43–0.81). DISCUSSION Sensorimotor

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: lower odds of MCI: ARIC odds ratio (OR) = 0.53 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.40–0.71); BLSA OR = 0.59 (95% CI: 0.43–0.81). DISCUSSION Sensorimotor function appears robustly related with MCI in a large sample of older adults. These findings highlight the potential value of incorporating sensorimotor assessments in early detection for cognitive decline. Longitudinal research is needed to understand temporality.

text: 2 METHODS 2.1 Study design and participants 2.1.1 The ARIC study The ARIC study is a prospective cohort study conducted across four US communities, including Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Jackson, Mississippi, where only Black participants were enrolled. The study enrolled 15,792 men and women aged 45 to 64 years at baseline (1987–1989) and was initiated to explore the mechanisms of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular risk factors. Evaluation was conducted twice per participant, 3 years apart. 24 The present analysis used data collected during the sixth ARIC examination (conducted in 2016–2017). At the sixth visit, 3699 individuals completed assessments of motor and physical function. Among this group, 957 participants also underwent vision testing as part of the Eye Determinants of Cognition (EyeDOC) ancillary study from the Washington County and Jackson sites. They also completed hearing and smell evaluations. Participants who

text: Cognition (EyeDOC) ancillary study from the Washington County and Jackson sites. They also completed hearing and smell evaluations. Participants who identified as neither White nor Black were excluded ( n = 4 Asian participants). Individuals with a prior history of stroke ( n = 38), Parkinson's disease ( n = 4), or Alzheimer's disease ( n = 21) were also excluded. Further, nine participants without measures on body mass index (BMI) and one participant without reported education were also excluded. The sample for this analysis was 880 men and women who were evaluated between June 2016 and December 2017 (Figure S1 in supporting information). This study adhered to the ethical guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki. Institutional review board approval was obtained, and each participant provided written informed consent. This ongoing cohort study enrolls community‐dwelling adults to investigate how aging and disease interact and affect physical and cognitive function. Participants must be free of major chronic illnesses and cognitive and functional impairments at enrollment. Participants are followed for life through clinical or home visits as needed, scheduled every 4 years for those < 60 years, every 2 years for those aged 60 to 79 years, and annually for those ≥ 80 years. 26 In 2003, the study was redesigned to use clear criteria for selecting healthy participants and to collect more detailed information on different aspects of their health. 27 All measures undergo quality control procedures and only valid data for this study were shared for analyses. 28 Longitudinal data

Additionally, 1091 participants completed sensory testing, including hearing, vision, and olfaction, resulting in 2704 observations between January 2012 and July 2019. For cross‐sectional analysis, only data from each participant's most recent visit were used when participants had all available data on sensorimotor functioning. Participants were excluded if they were under age 50 years ( n = 95) or had a prior history of stroke, Parkinson's disease, or non‐amnestic cognitive impairment ( n = 39). After further excluding participants with dementia ( n = 8), the final analysis comprised 681 participants (Figure S2 in supporting information). The institutional review board of the intramural

The institutional review board of the intramural research program of the National Institutes of Health approved the study protocol. At each visit, each participant provided written informed consent. 2.2 Sensory function 2.2.1 Hearing In ARIC, pure tone air conduction audiometry was performed in a sound‐treated booth at visit 6 (2016–2017). 29 Trained technicians measured air conduction thresholds for each ear at standard octave frequencies ranging from 0.5 to 8 kHz, using insert earphones and an Interacoustics AD629 audiometer. 30 Pure tone average (PTA) was derived by averaging four frequencies at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 kHz in the better‐hearing ear. Hearing loss was defined as PTA > 25 dB hearing loss in the better‐hearing ear based on those commonly used in population research. 31 RESEARCH IN CONTEXT Systematic review : The authors conducted a comprehensive review of literature via PubMed and

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: used in population research. 31 RESEARCH IN CONTEXT Systematic review : The authors conducted a comprehensive review of literature via PubMed and conference proceedings to evaluate the relationships among sensory, motor, and cognitive function. While previous studies often assessed individual sensory or motor impairments in relation to cognitive decline, none have proposed a unified sensorimotor construct and assess its role in cognitive health. Interpretation : This study developed and validated a novel sensorimotor function score across two large aging cohorts using common and non‐threatening tests. Findings show that higher sensorimotor function is associated with lower mild cognitive impairment (MCI) risk in older adults, suggesting that the integration of motor and sensory function is a meaningful marker of early cognitive decline. Future directions : Future research is needed to replicate findings and conduct longitudinal studies to establish the temporal relationship between

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: Future directions : Future research is needed to replicate findings and conduct longitudinal studies to establish the temporal relationship between changes in sensorimotor function and MCI onset and progression. PTA measured in BLSA was conducted in the same manner, except the standard octaves ranged from 0.5 kHz to 4 kHz. 32 2.2.2 Vision In ARIC, vision was assessed using a combination of visual acuity and contrast sensitivity measures. 33 Distance visual acuity was assessed by having participants read letters from a backlit ETDRS (Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study) chart while wearing their usual corrective lenses, if applicable. An autorefractor was also used to measure refraction and corrected visual acuity. 34 , 35 , 36 Impaired presenting visual acuity was defined as a visual acuity < 20/40, which is equivalent to logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (logMAR) values > 0.30. Contrast sensitivity was assessed using the Mars letter contrast sensitivity test while

text: of the minimum angle of resolution (logMAR) values > 0.30. Contrast sensitivity was assessed using the Mars letter contrast sensitivity test while participants wore their usual corrective lenses. 37 Impaired contrast sensitivity was defined as a score more than one standard deviation below the sample mean, with logContrast < 1.48 measured unilaterally using the Mars chart, in accordance with established thresholds. 38 In BLSA, composite visual impairment was defined as having impairment in any one of the following: contrast sensitivity, visual fields, visual acuity, and stereo acuity. 33 Beginning in January 2015, the BLSA vision protocol was updated to measure visual acuity unilaterally at a 3 meter distance using ETDRS eye charts (Precision Vision), with participants wearing their usual corrective lenses. 14 Better‐eye presenting visual acuity was assessed using the ETDRS chart, which determined whether the participant can correctly identify at least three of five letters.

Impairment was defined as visual acuity < 20/40, consistent with commonly used clinical and research criteria. 39 Contrast sensitivity was assessed bilaterally using the Pelli–Robson chart, reported in logContrast units, with participants wearing their corrective lenses when applicable. 14 , 40 Contrast sensitivity impairment was defined as a logContrast score < 1.55, representing one standard deviation below the average reported in previous population‐based studies of adults aged ≥ 60 years. 39 , 41 Visual fields were assessed using the Humphrey Field Analyzer (Carl Zeiss Meditec) with an 81‐point, single‐intensity (24 dB) full field test covering 60°. Monocular visual fields were assessed directly, while binocular visual fields were estimated using a previously established method. 42 Composite binocular visual fields were scored based on

text: while binocular visual fields were estimated using a previously established method. 42 Composite binocular visual fields were scored based on the total number of missed points out of 96, comprising 56 points in the central field, 18 in the upper peripheral field, and 22 in the lower peripheral field. Impairment was defined as a score exceeding one standard deviation above the cohort mean for total points missed. Stereo acuity, assessed using the Randot Stereo Vision Test, was considered impaired if participants were unable to discern a depth differential of more than 85 seconds of arc. 43 2.2.3 Olfaction In ARIC, olfactory function was assessed at visit 5 using the 12‐item Sniffin’ Sticks Odor Identification Test, with 1 point awarded for each correctly identified odorant for a maximum score of 12. 44 Olfactory impairment was defined as a total score of ≤ 6, in accordance with established thresholds of the 10th percentile. 45 In BLSA, olfaction was assessed using the 16‐item Sniffin’

text: a total score of ≤ 6, in accordance with established thresholds of the 10th percentile. 45 In BLSA, olfaction was assessed using the 16‐item Sniffin’ Sticks Odor Identification Test. 46 Two versions of the test were randomly used at the initial assessment and then alternated at follow‐up visits. Due to the absence of established impairment thresholds in the literature, impaired olfaction was defined as a score of ≤ 8 on test A and ≤ 7 on test B, corresponding to the 11th percentile of each test version within the current sample. 39 2.3 Motor function In both ARIC and BLSA, physical functioning was assessed using the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), 47 , 48 which includes full tandem stance (FTS) balance tests (held for 10 seconds in ARIC and 30 seconds for BLSA), five repeated chair stands performed as quickly as possible, and usual gait speed (UGS). Notably, gait speed was measured over a 4‐meter course in ARIC, whereas a 6‐meter course was used in BLSA. UGS was classified

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: usual gait speed (UGS). Notably, gait speed was measured over a 4‐meter course in ARIC, whereas a 6‐meter course was used in BLSA. UGS was classified as fast if it exceeded 0.8 m/s in ARIC, based on the sample's data distribution, and 1.0 m/s in BLSA. 47 The ability and duration to maintain each standing balance pose were recorded. For the FTS, the binary indicator reflected the ability to hold each pose for the full 10 or 30 seconds. Chair stand performance was quantified as the rate of stands per second. The cutoff for chair stand pace (CSP) was defined as > 0.28 stands per second in ARIC and > 0.44 stands per second (representing the lowest quintile) in BLSA, based on the current sample data distribution. 49 , 50 In both ARIC and BLSA, hand grip strength was assessed in kilograms using a Jamar hydraulic hand dynamometer. 51 Three trials were performed on each hand, and the highest measurement from either the left or right hand was used for analysis. Cutoffs for normal grip strength

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: were performed on each hand, and the highest measurement from either the left or right hand was used for analysis. Cutoffs for normal grip strength were set at 32 kg for men and 20 kg for women, consistent with thresholds used previously. 52 2.4 MCI MCI was determined through an evaluation of neuropsychological test results. In the ARIC study, the diagnosis of MCI was determined using criteria based on the National Institute on Aging–Alzheimer's Association (NIA‐AA) workgroups and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM‐5). A classification committee evaluated participants identified with MCI by algorithm. The diagnosis was confirmed by two independent reviewers, a neurologist and a neuropsychologist, while a third reviewer resolved any discrepancies when needed. 44 In BLSA, consensus diagnoses of cognitive impairment are made collaboratively by a multidisciplinary research team that includes neurologists, neuropsychologists, research nurses, and

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: impairment are made collaboratively by a multidisciplinary research team that includes neurologists, neuropsychologists, research nurses, and research assistants, 53 using neuropsychological testing and clinical data. MCI is diagnosed using the Petersen criteria, which require evidence of cognitive impairment in one or more domains without significant decline in the ability to perform activities of daily living. 53 , 54 , 55 2.5 Covariates Sociodemographic characteristics, including age, race, sex, and education level (college or higher), were self‐reported during the health interview. BMI was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared (kg/m 2 ). Self‐reported chronic conditions included cardiovascular disease, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and cancer. The number of comorbidities were classified as less than two versus two or more conditions. Depressive symptoms were measured as ≥ 9 on the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression (CES‐D) 11‐item

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: than two versus two or more conditions. Depressive symptoms were measured as ≥ 9 on the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression (CES‐D) 11‐item questionnaire for the ARIC study 56 and ≥ 20 on the CES‐D 30‐item questionnaire for BLSA. 57 2.6 Statistical approach Means and standard deviations (SD) or frequencies and percentages were calculated for demographic characteristics and sensorimotor function measures. Structural equation modeling (SEM) allows constructs to be represented as latent variables by capturing the shared covariation among indicators within a measurement model. This method typically results in less measurement error compared to using algebraic composites or sum scores. 58 A unidimensional sensorimotor functioning construct was derived using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in ARIC. Model fit was assessed using absolute fit indices, including the comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: using absolute fit indices, including the comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker–Lewis Index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). Criteria for excellent model fit were defined as CFI ≥ 0.95, TLI ≥ 0.95, RMSEA ≤ 0.05, and SRMR ≤ 0.08. 59 The initial CFA model included seven binary indicators of sensory and motor function: hearing, vision, olfaction, FTS balance, five‐repeat CSP, UGS, and grip strength, with higher values reflecting better functioning. To achieve a more parsimonious model, a leave‐one‐out approach was applied. This final CFA model retained six binary indicators: hearing, vision, olfaction, FTS balance, UGS, and usual grip strength. This final model was selected based on improved model fit indices and more evenly distributed factor loadings across indicators. Cross‐cohort measurement invariance of the latent construct sensorimotor score was evaluated using multi‐group confirmatory factor analysis with

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: Cross‐cohort measurement invariance of the latent construct sensorimotor score was evaluated using multi‐group confirmatory factor analysis with weighted least squares mean and variance (WLSMV) adjusted estimation for binary indicators. Models were fit sequentially starting with configural invariance (same factor structure across cohorts) and then scalar invariance (equality constraints appropriate for categorical indicators). Model fit was assessed using RMSEA, CFI, TLI, and SRMR. Because WLSMV chi‐squared values are not differenced in the usual way, nested model comparisons were conducted using the DIFFTEST procedure. When full scalar invariance was rejected, partial scalar invariance models were evaluated by freeing theoretically and empirically supported non‐invariant thresholds identified via modification indices. Improvement in model fit was confirmed using DIFFTEST. Separate logistic regression models were constructed to estimate the association between the sensorimotor

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: in model fit was confirmed using DIFFTEST. Separate logistic regression models were constructed to estimate the association between the sensorimotor functioning construct and each individual sensory and motor component with MCI. These models were used to evaluate the absolute standardized effect sizes with MCI. Receiver operating curves were also constructed to evaluate discriminatory ability (area under the curve) of the sensorimotor functioning construct and each individual sensory and motor component for MCI status. After establishing acceptable fit of the measurement model in ARIC, the unidimensional sensorimotor functioning construct was modeled as an exogenous variable (predictor), with MCI as the endogenous outcome. The full model was adjusted for age, race, sex, education, and BMI. The association between the latent sensorimotor functioning factor and MCI was estimated using probit regression, and the resulting coefficients were converted to odds ratios (ORs) for the binary

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: functioning factor and MCI was estimated using probit regression, and the resulting coefficients were converted to odds ratios (ORs) for the binary outcome by multiplying each coefficient by a scaling factor of 1.7 and then exponentiating it to approximate ORs derived from logistic regression. 60 A sensitivity analysis was performed to further adjust for self‐reported cardiovascular disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, cancer, diabetes, and depressive symptoms as potential confounders. A significance level of α = 0.05 was used for all analyses. Descriptive statistics were calculated using R version 4.1.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing), while SEM was carried out using Mplus version 8.4 (Muthén & Muthén).

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: 4 DISCUSSION Comprehensive evaluation of sensorimotor function may prove a useful non‐threatening potential early marker of present or emerging MCI. The results were consistent between two cohorts of older adults who together represent a wide range of low‐ to well‐functioning older adults without high morbidity burden. Importantly, our study suggests the key role that sensorimotor function may play in cognitive impairment. Future research to understand whether changes in sensorimotor function underlie the etiology of MCI is warranted. Our findings suggest a robust relationship between sensorimotor function and MCI, supporting current evidence that underscores the importance of multisensory integration in cognitive health. 19 In 2024, our group published evidence showing that components of sensorimotor function, including multisensory impairment and fine motor movement, are linked with early cognitive impairment—a state preceding mild cognitive impairment. 39 Also, Schubert et al.

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: impairment and fine motor movement, are linked with early cognitive impairment—a state preceding mild cognitive impairment. 39 Also, Schubert et al. showed that including mid‐life sensory and motor functioning improved risk prediction of 10‐year cognitive decline or impairment. 23 Together, this suggests a potential casual pathway, whereby declines in sensorimotor function might precede if not contribute to cognitive deficits. 39 As both findings are from cross‐sectional study designs, longitudinal studies will be required to reveal the temporality of this relationship. Traditionally, sensorimotor assessments such as threshold detection of passive motion, joint position reproduction, and active movement extent discrimination primarily focused on proprioceptive function. 61 , 62 However, these tests often overlook broader sensory functions, including hearing and olfaction. Our approach integrates commonly performed sensory and motor tests, encompassing hearing, vision, olfaction,

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: including hearing and olfaction. Our approach integrates commonly performed sensory and motor tests, encompassing hearing, vision, olfaction, standing balance, UGS, and hand grip strength. Balance is linked with postural control and cognitive resource engagement in complex environments. 63 Grip strength potentially captures neuromuscular coordination and functional reaching of the upper body. 64 Usual walking speed reflects mobility and cognitive processing during the planning and execution of spatial navigation. 65 Hearing is involved with enhancing spatial awareness by informing navigation through auditory cues. 66 Vision plays a role in spatial orientation and environmental awareness, likely influencing both locomotion and cognitive load during movement. 67 , 68 Last, olfactory sensations are linked to cognitive processes like impulsivity and inhibitory control that may influence sensorimotor function and behavior. 69 Collectively, these components highlight the non‐threatening as

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: and inhibitory control that may influence sensorimotor function and behavior. 69 Collectively, these components highlight the non‐threatening as well as informative nature of these sensorimotor assessments that may be important for screening for earlier identification of cognitive impairment and possibly intervention/corrective action. We selected and evaluated a 6‐indicator model of sensorimotor functioning that included auditory (hearing), visual (vision), olfactory (olfaction), postural stability (standing balance), locomotion (UGS), and upper body strength (grip strength). The 6‐indicator model, which replaced grip strength with CSP, exhibited arguably equivalent model fit. A notable distinction between the two models was that the model with CSP demonstrated a lower factor loading for hearing and a higher loading for UGS. One possible explanation for these differences is that the relationship between hearing and lower extremity performance, which includes gait speed, may be

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: explanation for these differences is that the relationship between hearing and lower extremity performance, which includes gait speed, may be moderated by cognitive processes 70 that control timing and coordination of movement. 50 Another reason is that grip strength may reflect discrete upper extremity functionality, representing aspects of fine motor skills and cognitive engagement that do not overlap with the relationship between hearing and mobility. 71 While both models exhibit slight variations in their relationships among the indicators of sensorimotor functioning, their comparable overall fit suggests that either model may be acceptable for preventive efforts or clinical use. Although full scalar invariance was not supported, partial scalar invariance was achieved by freeing the threshold of one indicator, supporting meaningful latent‐level comparisons across cohorts. The observed non‐invariance was primarily attributable to structural differences in task protocols and

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: latent‐level comparisons across cohorts. The observed non‐invariance was primarily attributable to structural differences in task protocols and resulting ceiling effects. Specifically, the shorter administration of FTS held in 10 seconds in BLSA, combined with its younger and healthier profile, rendered the task too easy, leading to near‐universal success, collapsed discrimination, and a shifted effective threshold. In contrast, the longer and more challenging FTS held for 30 seconds protocol in BLSA preserved response variability and functioned more stably across cohorts, thereby anchoring the latent scale more effectively. Additional contributors to differential item functioning may include differences in age distributions, cohort health status, and selection processes. Together, these findings highlight the importance of aligning measurement difficulty with cohort characteristics and demonstrate the value of partial invariance approaches for maintaining construct comparability when

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: difficulty with cohort characteristics and demonstrate the value of partial invariance approaches for maintaining construct comparability when localized, protocol‐driven measurement differences are present. Our study has limitations. First, the temporality of the relationship between sensorimotor function and MCI cannot be determined due to the cross‐sectional design. Second, several traditionally used sensory and motor measures such as proprioception, temperature, and muscle tone were not included in our evaluation. 72 Third, while we conducted analyses in ARIC and BLSA cohorts to increase external validity of the sensorimotor construct, the generalizability of the results may not extend to minoritized or historically underrepresented populations. Fourth, there are different confounding structures for many of the exposures that were combined into the sensorimotor construct. Fifth, there is a possibility for residual confounding. Sixth, mean sensorimotor score differences between ARIC

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: into the sensorimotor construct. Fifth, there is a possibility for residual confounding. Sixth, mean sensorimotor score differences between ARIC and BLSA due to cohort variability (e.g., differing study methods to evaluate both sensorimotor function and MCI) should be acknowledged. Seventh, dichotomizing indicators of sensorimotor function as impaired or unimpaired potentially discards important information (e.g., dose–response). Eighth, the low MCI prevalence in both cohorts may attenuate the magnitude of association between sensorimotor function and MCI toward the null and is likely greater in populations with higher MCI prevalence. The strengths of this study include the use of large, well‐characterized cohorts and the inclusion of multiple objectively measured sensory and motor measures. In conclusion, our study provides evidence that higher sensorimotor function measured with commonly used assessments is associated with a lower risk of MCI. The integration of sensory and motor

title: A sensorimotor function construct to assess mild cognitive impairment risk
text: higher sensorimotor function measured with commonly used assessments is associated with a lower risk of MCI. The integration of sensory and motor abilities may play a role in cognitive impairment during the early stage of MCI, highlighting the importance of maintaining sensory and motor health as part of a broader and preventive strategy against cognitive decline. Longitudinal studies are warranted to replicate our findings and to assess temporality of the relationship of sensorimotor function with MCI, above and beyond its individual sensory and motor components.

title: Histone Modifications in Cardiovascular Disease: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities
text: ABSTRACT Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of death worldwide. Maladaptive transcriptional programs drive the fibrosis, hypertrophy, and vascular inflammation that characterize these pathologies. Histone posttranslational modifications regulate these programs by remodeling chromatin accessibility and transcriptional output in cardiomyocytes, vascular cells, and immune cells. These modifications include methylation, acetylation, and metabolite‐derived acylations. While the enzymatic machinery of classical histone marks is increasingly well defined, the cell‐type‐specific integration of these regulators into dynamic cardiovascular networks remains incompletely understood. This narrative review summarizes experimental and human studies published up to early 2026. We examine how classical marks such as H3K27me3 and H3K9ac, alongside emerging metabolic sensors like histone lysine lactylation, shape core pathobiological programs, including oxidative stress responses,

title: Histone Modifications in Cardiovascular Disease: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities
text: alongside emerging metabolic sensors like histone lysine lactylation, shape core pathobiological programs, including oxidative stress responses, endothelial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix remodeling, across major cardiovascular syndromes. We further critically evaluate the enzymatic machinery and pharmacological strategies by contrasting broad‐spectrum histone deacetylase inhibition with precision approaches, including bromodomain inhibition and locus‐selective epigenome editing. Finally, we address translational constraints such as drug delivery and off‐target effects. We propose that single‐cell resolution and spatial multiomics will be essential to identify compartment‐specific targets and advance precision cardiovascular epigenetic therapeutics.

title: Ocular Surgery in Patients With Severe Atherosclerotic Disease: Anesthetic Considerations and Vascular Risk Stratification
text: Ocular surgery in patients with severe atherosclerotic disease represents a growing clinical challenge due to the increasing prevalence of cardiovascular comorbidities in aging populations. Atherosclerosis, characterized by endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and arterial stiffness, compromises vascular autoregulation and reduces ocular perfusion, thereby increasing susceptibility to ischemic complications during perioperative hemodynamic fluctuations. In this context, patients undergoing ophthalmic procedures, even those considered low risk, such as cataract surgery, may experience significant cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events. A comprehensive preoperative evaluation is essential and should include detailed cardiovascular history, functional capacity assessment, frailty evaluation, and the use of validated risk indices. Targeted investigations such as electrocardiography, echocardiography, and carotid Doppler imaging allow for the identification of high-risk features and

title: Ocular Surgery in Patients With Severe Atherosclerotic Disease: Anesthetic Considerations and Vascular Risk Stratification
text: investigations such as electrocardiography, echocardiography, and carotid Doppler imaging allow for the identification of high-risk features and guide perioperative planning. The management of antithrombotic therapy requires an individualized approach that balances thrombotic and bleeding risks, particularly in patients receiving dual antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation. The choice of anesthetic technique plays a critical role in maintaining hemodynamic stability. Techniques with minimal systemic impact, such as topical anesthesia and Sub-Tenon block, are generally preferred, while general anesthesia should be reserved for selected cases. Intraoperatively, maintaining stable mean arterial pressure, avoiding hypotension and hypertension, and ensuring normocapnia are key strategies to preserve cerebral and ocular perfusion. Postoperative care should focus on early detection of myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, and neurological complications, as well as timely resumption of

title: Ocular Surgery in Patients With Severe Atherosclerotic Disease: Anesthetic Considerations and Vascular Risk Stratification
text: care should focus on early detection of myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, and neurological complications, as well as timely resumption of antithrombotic therapy. Ultimately, a multidisciplinary and individualized approach is essential to optimize perioperative safety and improve outcomes in this high-risk population.

title: Ocular Surgery in Patients With Severe Atherosclerotic Disease: Anesthetic Considerations and Vascular Risk Stratification
text: Conclusions Ocular surgery in patients with severe atherosclerotic disease carries a significant risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and ocular complications due to the interaction between endothelial dysfunction, impaired vascular autoregulation, and decreased ocular perfusion. Therefore, rigorous preoperative risk stratification, along with optimization of risk factors and appropriate selection of anesthetic techniques, is essential to reduce adverse events and improve clinical outcomes. Perioperative management in this population must be comprehensive and multidisciplinary, focusing on intraoperative hemodynamic control, continuous monitoring, balancing thrombotic and hemorrhagic risk, and early detection of postoperative complications. These strategies minimize the risk of cerebral and ocular ischemia and optimize safety in complex clinical settings.

title: Rationale and design of the Early Initiation of Intensification Lipid-Lowering Treatment in Acute Coronary Syndrome (ELITE-ACS): a real-world study
text: OBJECTIVE To investigate the effects of early in-hospital intensive lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) with proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors on lipid dynamics and clinical outcomes in Chinese acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients, providing robust real-world evidence for its long-term benefits and optimal implementation timing to address the evidence gap in optimal lipid management for secondary prevention. METHODS & RESULTS This multicenter prospective real-world study ( http://www.clinicaltrials.gov , NCT number: NCT06738758 ), which building upon the ELEGANT pilot registry (ChiCTR2200065861), will enroll 6000 consecutively hospitalized ACS patients with uncontrolled dyslipidemia across more than 30 Chinese centers. Participants are enrolled based on recommended stratified proportions [(1) diagnostic categories: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction : non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction : intermediate-high-risk unstable angina = 1:1:3; and

title: Rationale and design of the Early Initiation of Intensification Lipid-Lowering Treatment in Acute Coronary Syndrome (ELITE-ACS): a real-world study
text: ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction : non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction : intermediate-high-risk unstable angina = 1:1:3; and (2) lipid-lowering strategies: PCSK9 inhibitor ± statin : statin+ezetimibe/hybutimibe : statin = 2:1:2). Treatment assignment reflects real-world clinical decisions guided by low-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels and patient preference. Twelve-month follow-up assessments were conducted at predefined intervals: baseline hospitalization, discharge, and 1, 3, 6, 12 months post-discharge. Primary endpoints were the goal attainment (low-density lipoprotein cholesterol < 1.4 mmol/L) rates across treatment arms. Key secondary endpoints were the major adverse cardiovascular events (including myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, cardiovascular mortality, coronary revascularization) and all-cause death, and other secondary endpoints encompassed time-to-lipid-goal, longitudinal changes in lipids profiles and inflammatory biomarkers, and

title: Rationale and design of the Early Initiation of Intensification Lipid-Lowering Treatment in Acute Coronary Syndrome (ELITE-ACS): a real-world study
text: death, and other secondary endpoints encompassed time-to-lipid-goal, longitudinal changes in lipids profiles and inflammatory biomarkers, and perivascular fat attenuation index evolution quantified by coronary computed tomographic angiography. Propensity score matching and inverse probability treatment weighting will address confounding bias. CONCLUSIONS This study will pioneer evidence clarifying the optimal therapeutic window and clinical benefits of in-hospital intensive LLT for Chinese ACS patients. By establishing the first Chinese population-derived evidence for the “early intensive and rapid target attainment” strategy, our findings may challenge stepwise LLT paradigms. These results may guide international guideline updates for high-risk ACS populations, particularly in East Asian cohorts with distinct lipid profiles.

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: Objective To investigate the association between sarcopenia and ventricular remodelling after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in elderly patients with coronary heart disease (CHD). Methods A total of 135 elderly patients with CHD admitted to hospital between February 2021 and May 2023 were prospectively selected. According to whether ventricular remodelling occurred during the follow-up period, patients were divided into an occurrence group and a non-occurrence group. Results The incidence of ventricular remodelling after CABG in elderly patients with CHD was 23.70% (32/135). Significant differences between the two groups were observed in smoking history, diabetes history, prevalence of sarcopenia, degree of preoperative coronary stenosis, levels of lipoprotein (a) ([Lp(a)]), uric acid (UA), protease-activated receptor 2 (PAR2), monocyte-to-HDL ratio (MHR), and suspended red blood cell input ( P < 0.05). Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified smoking history [odds

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: ratio (MHR), and suspended red blood cell input ( P < 0.05). Multivariable logistic regression analysis identified smoking history [odds ratio (OR) = 2.186, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.34–3.57], diabetes history (OR = 2.171, 95% CI 1.32–3.58), sarcopenia (OR = 2.230, 95% CI 1.37–3.62), a high degree of preoperative coronary stenosis (OR = 2.223, 95% CI 1.36–3.64), elevated Lp(a) (OR = 2.143, 95% CI 1.32–3.49), elevated UA (OR = 2.164, 95% CI 1.31–3.58), elevated PAR2 (OR = 2.192, 95% CI 1.32–3.64), and elevated MHR (OR = 2.201, 95% CI 1.32–3.68) as independent risk factors for ventricular remodelling after CABG in the study population. Analysis showed that sarcopenia predicted ventricular remodelling with a sensitivity of 90.0%, specificity of 47.0%, and an area under the curve of 0.772 (95% CI 0.68–0.86, P < 0.0001). Conclusion Sarcopenia is a risk factor affecting ventricular remodelling after CABG in elderly patients and shows strong predictive efficacy in this population.

text: 2 Methods 2.1 Criteria for the assessment of sarcopenia The diagnosis of sarcopenia followed the consensus recommendations of the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2 (2019) ( 15 ) and the Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (2019) ( 16 ). The diagnostic framework included 3 components: low muscle mass, low muscle strength, and low physical performance. In our study, the following cutoffs were applied: (1) relative skeletal muscle mass index (SMI): <7.0 kg/m² for men and <5.7 kg/m² for women, (2) handgrip strength (dominant hand): <26 kg for men and <18 kg for women, and (3) gait speed: <0.8 m/s for both men and women. Participants with low muscle mass [criterion (1)] combined with either low muscle strength [criterion (2)] or low physical performance [criterion (3)] were classified as having sarcopenia. 2.2 Criteria for assessment of ventricular remodelling Echocardiography was performed using a diagnostic echocardiograph to record LVEDV. The LVEDV growth rate was

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: assessment of ventricular remodelling Echocardiography was performed using a diagnostic echocardiograph to record LVEDV. The LVEDV growth rate was calculated from two echocardiographic measurements as follows: Δ LVEDV = ( second LVEDV − first LVEDV / first LVEDV ) × 100 % . A ΔLVEDV ≥15% was defined as ventricular remodelling, consistent with existing literature, demonstrating its prognostic significance (e.g., hazard ratio: 2.1, P = 0.007) ( 8 , 17 , 18 ). 2.3 Follow-up and grouping Following surgery, patients received regular follow-ups until November 2023. The median follow-up duration was 12 months (range, 6–18 months), conducted through a combination of outpatient visits and telephone interviews. Standardised echocardiographic assessments were performed at baseline (within 1 week after surgery) and at 3, 6, and 12 months, with additional evaluations if cardiac symptoms occurred. According to the criteria in section 1.3.2, patients who developed ventricular remodelling during the

text: evaluations if cardiac symptoms occurred. According to the criteria in section 1.3.2, patients who developed ventricular remodelling during the follow-up period were included in the occurrence group, and the rest were included in the non-occurrence group. Clinical data were compared between the two groups. 2.4 Clinical data collection Patient data during hospitalisation were retrieved from the hospital's electronic medical record system by a single nurse who was blinded to the patient grouping. The records included the following data: general information (gender, age, body mass index, history of smoking and alcohol consumption, past medical history [hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia], and presence of sarcopenia; lesion characteristics (location, type, branching, degree of coronary artery stenosis); biochemical profiles at admission (total cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)], aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase,

To assess the association between sarcopenia and postoperative ventricular remodelling, multivariable logistic regression models were fitted. Candidate predictors with clinical relevance and/or P < 0.10 in univariate analyses were entered simultaneously into the multivariable model to obtain adjusted ORs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Continuous predictors (e.g., Lp(a), UA, monocyte count, MHR) were z-standardised (value–mean)/SD before modelling to place coefficients on a comparable scale, and categorical covariates (e.g., smoking, diabetes, sarcopenia) were dichotomised using predefined criteria. text: 1.1 Information and methods 1.1.1 Sample size justification Before enrolment, an a priori power calculation for the primary endpoint (post-CABG ventricular remodelling, defined as ΔLVEDV ≥ 15%) was performed. Assuming a remodelling incidence of 30% in the overall cohort, an expected risk increase associated with sarcopenia corresponding to an odds ratio (OR) = 2.0, two-sided α = 0.05, and 80% power, the minimum required sample size was approximately 128 participants to provide a balanced and effective sample for logistic regression. To allow for potential loss to follow-up and measurement uncertainty, the target sample size was set at ≥130 participants. The final cohort included 135 patients, meeting the prespecified power requirement. 1.1.2 General information A total of 135 elderly patients with CHD who were admitted to hospital between February 2021 and May 2023 were prospectively selected. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥60 years, (2) diagnosis of CHD confirmed by

text: February 2021 and May 2023 were prospectively selected. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age ≥60 years, (2) diagnosis of CHD confirmed by coronary angiography, (3) fulfilment of surgical indications for CABG and successful completion of the procedure, (4) adherence to prescribed postoperative medication, and (5) provision of signed informed consent for study participation. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) active bleeding, gastrointestinal haemorrhage, or cerebral haemorrhage within the past 3 months; (2) history of cardiogenic syncope, cardiogenic shock, or severe cardiac arrhythmia; (3) the presence of a malignant tumour, severe immune system disease, or hepatic or renal insufficiency; and (4) the presence of cognitive dysfunction, bipolar disorder, or other psychiatric disorders. The hospital ethics committee reviewed and approved the study protocol prior to implementation.

text: 4 Discussion In this study, we found that the proportion of sarcopenia in the ventricular remodelling group was significantly higher than in the non-occurrence group, and multivariate regression analysis confirmed that sarcopenia was independently associated with ventricular remodelling after CABG in elderly patients with CHD. These results are consistent with previous reports ( 12 – 14 ), supporting the view that sarcopenia not only increases frailty but also adversely affects cardiac structure and function. Our findings highlight the clinical importance of recognising sarcopenia as a risk factor for adverse cardiac remodelling in elderly patients undergoing CABG. Incorporating sarcopenia assessment into perioperative evaluation may help identify high-risk patients, guide nutritional and rehabilitation interventions and, ultimately, improve long-term outcomes. Existing studies have demonstrated that conventional biomarkers such as NT-proBNP are valuable predictors of adverse outcomes

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: long-term outcomes. Existing studies have demonstrated that conventional biomarkers such as NT-proBNP are valuable predictors of adverse outcomes after CABG. For example, elevated preoperative NT-proBNP levels have been associated with the development of postoperative left ventricular systolic dysfunction, showing moderate predictive utility (sensitivity 59%, specificity 80%) ( 19 ). A larger cohort study also identified postoperative elevations in NT-proBNP as independent predictors of postoperative heart failure, with significant ORs BioMed Central ( 20 ). Additionally, systematic reviews underscore the prognostic role of natriuretic peptides across a range of adverse cardiac outcomes following surgery ScienceDirect ( 21 ). In contrast, sarcopenia offers a distinct dimension of risk assessment. While NT-proBNP reflects acute myocardial stress and volume overload, sarcopenia integrates indicators of systemic nutritional status, muscle metabolism and frailty. In our study, sarcopenia

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: stress and volume overload, sarcopenia integrates indicators of systemic nutritional status, muscle metabolism and frailty. In our study, sarcopenia showed a robust predictive performance (AUC = 0.862, sensitivity 87.5%, specificity 76.5%), potentially providing complementary prognostic insight beyond conventional biomarkers. Incorporating sarcopenia assessment may, therefore, refine postoperative risk stratification and guide early rehabilitation interventions. Specifically, exercise-based rehabilitation, including both resistance and aerobic training, has emerged as the most effective non-pharmacologic intervention for sarcopenia ( 22 ). Resistance training can significantly enhance muscle strength, gait speed and functional performance in older adults with sarcopenia, especially when conducted at moderate-to-high intensity (≥60% one-repetition maximum) over a sustained period (≥8–12 weeks) ( 23 , 24 ). Moreover, aerobic and resistance exercise stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis,

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: maximum) over a sustained period (≥8–12 weeks) ( 23 , 24 ). Moreover, aerobic and resistance exercise stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis, reduce inflammation, improve insulin sensitivity and upregulate PGC-1 α , which may benefit not only muscle health but also cardiac remodelling processes ( 25 , 26 ). These mechanistic pathways dovetail with the associations we observed between sarcopenia and adverse ventricular remodelling (e.g., via insulin resistance and systemic inflammation), suggesting that exercise rehabilitation could favourably modulate postoperative cardiac structural adaptations. Future studies should explore whether tailored, combined exercise and nutritional interventions can attenuate ventricular remodelling and improve the long-term prognoses of elderly patients with CHD undergoing CABG. Sarcopenia plausibly links frailty, metabolic dysregulation, and inflammatory activation to adverse ventricular remodelling after CABG. Beyond a marker of aging, skeletal muscle is an

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: metabolic dysregulation, and inflammatory activation to adverse ventricular remodelling after CABG. Beyond a marker of aging, skeletal muscle is an endocrine organ; loss of muscle mass/strength shifts myokine balance, worsens insulin resistance, and reduces mitochondrial capacity, thereby amplifying surgical stress responses and susceptibility to remodelling ( 24 ). Within this framework, several convergent axes explain our findings: (i) Inflammation/innate immunity & endothelial dysfunction. Sarcopenia aligns with “inflammaging” monocyte activation, and impaired HDL anti-oxidative capacity. This favors endothelial activation and myocardial inflammatory signalling after surgery. The monocyte-to-HDL ratio (MHR) captures this imbalance and associates with vascular disease burden in contemporary cohorts ( 27 ). Coronary microvascular dysfunction, a consequence of endothelial injury and capillary rarefaction, promotes ischemia, diastolic stiffness, and fibrosis, all central to

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: dysfunction, a consequence of endothelial injury and capillary rarefaction, promotes ischemia, diastolic stiffness, and fibrosis, all central to postoperative remodelling ( 28 , 29 ). (ii) Metabolic inflexibility. Muscle loss reduces whole-body glucose disposal and mitochondrial oxidative flux, increasing ROS and lipotoxicity under peri-operative load. Exercise-responsive pathways (AMPK-PGC-1 α ) are down-tuned in sarcopenia; their re-engagement with training improves cardiometabolic efficiency and may counter adverse remodelling biology ( 30 – 32 ). (iii) Fibrosis signalling. Inflammation, oxidative stress, and RAAS activation converge on TGF-β/SMAD and matricellular nodes, driving collagen deposition and titin alterations that stiffen the ventricle ( 24 ). Our biomarkers fit this network as amplifiers rather than isolated correlates. Uric acid (UA) reflects xanthine-oxidase-mediated redox stress and is tightly linked to endothelial dysfunction and HF risk; UA-lowering contexts

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: Uric acid (UA) reflects xanthine-oxidase-mediated redox stress and is tightly linked to endothelial dysfunction and HF risk; UA-lowering contexts (e.g., SGLT2 inhibitor programs) further support a vascular-metabolic mechanism ( 33 , 34 ). Lp(a) carries oxidized phospholipids, promotes vascular inflammation, and impairs fibrinolysis, sustaining afterload/ischemia-two principal drivers of post-CABG remodelling ( 35 , 36 ). PAR-2 integrates protease-inflammation signalling, modulating endothelial permeability and NF-κB activity; experimental attenuation of PAR-2 reduces cardiac injury and inflammatory tone ( 37 , 38 ). MHR synthesizes monocyte activity against HDL antioxidation and tracks vascular calcific/inflammatory burden ( 27 ). Consistent with this biology, sarcopenia in our cohort provided stronger discrimination for postoperative remodelling than conventional acute-stress peptides, suggesting complementarity rather than redundancy. Clinically, two strategies emerge: (1) risk

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: remodelling than conventional acute-stress peptides, suggesting complementarity rather than redundancy. Clinically, two strategies emerge: (1) risk identification via sarcopenia screening (sex-specific SMI cut-offs) plus inflammatory/metabolic panels (UA, Lp(a), MHR, PAR-2); and (2) mechanism-informed intervention, combining progressive resistance and aerobic training-which up-regulates PGC-1α, improves insulin sensitivity, and dampens inflammatory signalling-with targeted metabolic/vascular therapy (e.g., XO/UA pathways; emerging Lp(a)-lowering) to blunt fibrosis and adverse LV geometry after CABG. Several previous studies ( 39 , 40 ) have shown that smoking not only promotes cell aggregation and increases endothelial cell viscosity but also reduces vascular high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels, damaging the arterial endothelium with multiple effects. The results of this study showed that smoking history was a risk factor for ventricular remodelling after CABG in elderly

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: with multiple effects. The results of this study showed that smoking history was a risk factor for ventricular remodelling after CABG in elderly patients with CHD, and the reasons for this may be related to the fact that tobacco contains nicotine and coal tar, which promote endothelial hyperplasia and oxidise free radicals in the blood vessels. Patients should be instructed to strictly abstain from smoking to prevent adverse cardiac events after surgery. Diabetes mellitus is an independent risk factor for ventricular remodelling after CABG in elderly patients with CHD. This could be attributed to the fact that advanced glycosylation end-products can mediate endothelial dysfunction, leading to vascular remodelling, thereby contributing to ventricular remodelling ( 41 ). It is expected that the risk of ventricular remodelling in elderly patients with CHD who have diabetes mellitus will be reduced if they are given a treatment targeting the glycosylation end-products after coronary

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: patients with CHD who have diabetes mellitus will be reduced if they are given a treatment targeting the glycosylation end-products after coronary bypass grafting(CABG) ( 42 ). The above suggests that the occurrence of ventricular remodelling after PCI in elderly patients with CHD is the result of a multifactorial effect, and it is expected to reduce the risk of ventricular remodelling after CABG by actively controlling the patient's underlying illnesses, following a doctor's instructions for taking medication and establishing good lifestyle habits. Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, although it adopted a prospective observational design, all data were obtained from a single centre, which may limit the generalisability of the findings. Second, the relatively small sample ( n = 135) may have reduced the statistical power to detect modest effects. Third, echocardiographic assessments of left ventricular volumes were performed by different sonographers at

title: Impact of sarcopenia on ventricular remodelling following coronary artery bypass grafting in elderly patients with coronary heart disease
text: power to detect modest effects. Third, echocardiographic assessments of left ventricular volumes were performed by different sonographers at separate time points, which may introduce measurement variability despite adherence to standardised imaging protocols and blinded analysis. Fourth, the median follow-up duration was only 12 months. Ventricular remodelling is a dynamic and often slow process that can evolve over several years; therefore, our results cannot determine whether the observed sarcopenia–remodelling association persists or strengthens beyond 1 year, nor can they clarify its relationship with long-term prognosis, such as survival, or recurrent major adverse cardiovascular events. Taken together, the single-centre design, limited sample size, and short follow-up duration restrict the external validity and prognostic extrapolation of our results. Future large-scale, multicentre, prospective cohorts with extended (≥5-year) follow-up and standardised echocardiographic
